Let \(\mathcal S\) be the functional (8.91) and \(f_1, \dots, f_{\mathrm{m}}\) functions that have continuous partial derivatives up to the second order on \([t_1, t_2] \times \mathbb R^n\), with \(m < n\). Let \(\vek q\) be an admissible function with \(f_{\mathrm{r}}(t, \vek q(t)) = 0\) for every \(r\) and every \(t\), for which the \(\hat F_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}}\) are continuously differentiable. Let the matrix \(\mat A(t)\) with entries \(A_{\mathrm{rs}}(t) = \frac{\partial f_{\mathrm{r}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\big(t, \vek q(t)\big)\) have \(m\) pivots for every \(t\) (as in theorem 8.95). We say that \(\vek q\) is stationary under the constraints (stacionarna točka pod vezmi) if \(\delta\mathcal S(\vek q, \vek\eta) = 0\) for every admissible variation \(\vek\eta\) for which \(\mat A(t)\,\vek\eta(t) = \vek 0\) for every \(t\). Then \(\vek q\) is stationary under the constraints if and only if there exist continuous functions \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) on \([t_1, t_2]\) that together with \(\vek q\) satisfy for every \(s\) the equations

\[\hat F_{\mathrm{q}_\mathrm{s}} - \frac{\mathrm{d}\hat F_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{d}t} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{m} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\frac{\partial f_{\mathrm{r}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} = 0 , \qquad f_{\mathrm{r}}(t, \vek q) = 0 . \tag{8.94}\]

The first are the equations of the Euler-Lagrange system (8.92) for the function \(F + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,f_{\mathrm{r}}\). The functions \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) are unique.

Proof

We must show both directions. One is a computation with the first variation. In the other, a projection onto tangent displacements gives variations that are continuously differentiable, and from the fundamental lemma we conclude that the column \(\vek E\) of theorem 8.98 is at every instant a linear combination of the rows of the matrix \(\mat A\).

  1. Let \(E_{\mathrm{s}}\) be as in theorem 8.98. Step 3 of its proof holds for every admissible variation, so \(\delta\mathcal S(\vek q, \vek\eta) = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \vek E\cdot\vek\eta\,\mathrm{d}t\) for the column \(\vek E = (E_1, \dots, E_{\mathrm{n}})\). Equation (8.94) says \(\vek E = -\mat A^\T\vek\lambda\) for the column \(\vek\lambda = (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{m}})\), since the derivative of the function \(F + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} f_{\mathrm{r}}\) with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is \(F_{\mathrm{q}_\mathrm{s}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\partial f_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\) and its derivative with respect to \(p_{\mathrm{s}}\) is \(F_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}}\), because \(f_{\mathrm{r}}\) does not contain \(\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  2. Let (8.94) hold and let \(\mat A\,\vek\eta = \vek 0\). Then \(\vek E\cdot\vek\eta = -(\mat A^\T\vek\lambda)\cdot\vek\eta = -\vek\lambda\cdot(\mat A\,\vek\eta) = 0\) at every instant, so \(\delta\mathcal S(\vek q, \vek\eta) = 0\). The function \(\vek q\) is stationary under the constraints.
  3. Conversely, let \(\vek q\) be stationary under the constraints. Let \(\mat K = \mat A\mat A^\T\), a matrix of order \(m\) for every \(t\). It is symmetric, because \((\mat A\mat A^\T)^\T = \mat A\mat A^\T\) (lemma 1.101). It is also positive definite: for \(\vek z \neq \vek 0\) we have \(\vek z^\T\mat K\vek z = (\mat A^\T\vek z)\cdot(\mat A^\T\vek z) = |\mat A^\T\vek z|^2 \ge 0\), and if \(\mat A^\T\vek z = \vek 0\) held, uniqueness in lemma 8.35 (for the column \(\vek a = \vek 0\), the matrix \(\mat A\) has \(m\) pivots) would give \(\vek z = \vek 0\). Hence \(\vek z^\T\mat K\vek z > 0\).
  4. The matrix \(\mat K\) is invertible and \(\mat K^{-1}\) is also a continuously differentiable function of time. The entries \(A_{\mathrm{rs}}(t) = \partial f_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}(t, \vek q(t))\) are continuously differentiable by the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 1), because \(f_{\mathrm{r}}\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(\vek q\) is continuously differentiable. The entries of the matrix \(\mat K\) are sums of products of these entries, so they are continuously differentiable (lemma 1.81). By lemma 8.99 the entries of the matrix \(\mat K^{-1}\) are therefore continuously differentiable.
  5. Let \(\mat P = \mat I - \mat A^\T\mat K^{-1}\mat A\), a matrix of size \(n \times n\) for every \(t\). We have \(\mat A\mat P = \mat A - \mat A\mat A^\T\mat K^{-1}\mat A = \mat A - \mat K\mat K^{-1}\mat A = \mat 0\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric, so \(\mat K^{-1}\) is symmetric as well (lemma 1.117) and \(\mat P^\T = \mat P\) (lemma 1.101). The entries of the matrix \(\mat P\) are sums of products of continuously differentiable functions, so \(\mat P\) is continuously differentiable.
  6. Choose \(s\) and a function \(\psi\) with a continuous derivative and \(\psi(t_1) = \psi(t_2) = 0\). The column \(\vek\eta = \psi\,\mat P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\) has by step 5 a continuous derivative, is zero at the end points, and \(\mat A\,\vek\eta = \psi\,\mat A\mat P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek 0\). It is therefore an admissible tangent variation, and by step 1 \(0 = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \psi\,\vek E\cdot\mat P\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}t = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \psi\,(\mat P\vek E)_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}t\), since \(\mat P\) is symmetric.
  7. The function \((\mat P\vek E)_{\mathrm{s}}\) is continuous, because \(\mat P\) and \(\vek E\) are continuous (\(E_{\mathrm{s}}\) is continuous as in step 5 of the proof of theorem 8.98). By the fundamental lemma (lemma 4.77) \((\mat P\vek E)_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) on \([t_1, t_2]\) for every \(s\), so \(\mat P\vek E = \vek 0\), that is, \(\vek E = \mat A^\T\mat K^{-1}\mat A\vek E\).
  8. Let \(\vek\lambda = -\mat K^{-1}\mat A\vek E\). It is continuous as a product of continuous functions, and by step 7 \(\vek E = -\mat A^\T\vek\lambda\), which is (8.94). If \(\vek\lambda'\) were another solution, we would have \(\mat A^\T(\vek\lambda - \vek\lambda') = \vek 0\), so by uniqueness in lemma 8.35 \(\vek\lambda = \vek\lambda'\).

Source: GR (1.77) to (1.82) (PDF pp. 62 to 63), EP (5.4.7), (5.4.11) (pp. 256, 257): the books choose the multipliers so that the coefficients of the dependent variations vanish, and state the ansatz without a proof of continuity. The proof by projection is not from a source. The algebraic statement that the column \(\vek E\) is orthogonal to all \(\vek\eta\) with \(\mat A\vek\eta = \vek 0\) if and only if \(\vek E = \mat A^\T\vek\lambda\) is lemma 8.35 at each instant separately. The projection only ensures that \(\vek\eta\) is continuously differentiable.

The sign of the multipliers is a convention: with \(F - \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} f_{\mathrm{r}}\) we would get \(-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). We chose \(+\) so that three sections agree. In section 8.3, \(\nabla V = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla f_{\mathrm{r}}\) holds (equation (8.21)). In theorem 8.95, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} - \partial\mathcal L/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} A_{\mathrm{rs}}\). For \(F = \mathcal L\) the left side is \(-E_{\mathrm{s}}\), so this is equation (8.94) with \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\). At rest \(\mathcal L = -V\), so \(E_{\mathrm{s}} = -\partial V/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\), and the same equation gives \(\nabla V = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla f_{\mathrm{r}}\). The multiplier \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) is thus everywhere the intensity of the reaction of constraint \(r\).

Let us test it on the pendulum with \(F = \tfrac12\,m\,(p_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + p_{\mathrm{y}}^2) - m\,g\,y\) (the kinetic energy minus the potential energy) and \(f = x^2 + y^2 - l^2\). The matrix \(\mat A = (2x,\ 2y)\) has one pivot, since the row is not zero: \(x^2 + y^2 = l^2 > 0\). Equations (8.94) are

\[-m\,\ddot x + 2\lambda\,x = 0 , \qquad -m\,g - m\,\ddot y + 2\lambda\,y = 0 .\]

We obtain the multiplier without solving the motion. The derivative of the constraint \(x\dot x + y\dot y = 0\) differentiated once more gives \(x\ddot x + y\ddot y = -(\dot x^2 + \dot y^2)\). We multiply the first equation by \(x\), the second by \(y\) and add: \(m\,(x\ddot x + y\ddot y) = 2\lambda\,(x^2 + y^2) - m\,g\,y\). With \(x = l\sin\theta\), \(y = -l\cos\theta\) and \(\dot x^2 + \dot y^2 = l^2\dot\theta^2\) this is \(-m\,l^2\dot\theta^2 = 2\lambda\,l^2 + m\,g\,l\cos\theta\), so

\[\lambda = -\frac{m}{2\,l}\,\big(l\,\dot\theta^2 + g\cos\theta\big) = -\frac{N}{2\,l} , \qquad N = m\,\big(g\cos\theta + l\,\dot\theta^2\big) .\]

The reaction of the constraint on the mass is \(2\lambda\,(x, y)\), a vector of magnitude \(2|\lambda|\,l = N\) that points towards the bearing when \(\lambda < 0\). \(N\) is thus the force in the rod, the same as in section 8.9. In a descent from rest at \(90°\) we have at the start \(\dot\theta = 0\), \(\cos\theta = 0\) and \(\lambda = 0\). At the bottom \(\dot\theta = 4{,}4294\) 1/s, so \(N = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot(9{,}81 + 1\ \text{m}\cdot 19{,}62\ \text{1/s}^2)\ \text{m/s}^2 = 29{,}43\) N and \(\lambda = -14{,}715\) N/m. The rod pulls, as it must.

For the bar we also need the fundamental lemma for functions of two variables \((x, t)\) on a rectangle. In section 4.2.2 we proved it as point 3 of lemma 4.83, for a rectangle in a plane of space. The name of the second variable does not matter in the statement, so we use it with \(t\) in place of \(y\) and need no new lemma.

8.10.3 The principle (načelo)

Now we have the tools for the answer. Let us write the number from the experiment as a definition. Let the system be described by \(n\) generalized coordinates \(\vek q\) (section 8.4), with kinetic energy \(T(t, \vek q, \dot{\vek q})\) (definition 8.79) and potential energy \(V(\vek q)\) from which the applied forces arise (definition 8.53).

Definition 8.101 Action integral (akcija)

Let \(\mathcal L(t, \vek q, \dot{\vek q}) = T - V\) be the Lagrangian (Lagrangeeva funkcija) of the system. The action (akcija) of the system on a path \(\vek q\), which is an admissible function of definition 8.97 on \([t_1, t_2]\), is the number

\[\mathcal S(\vek q) = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \mathcal L\big(t, \vek q(t), \dot{\vek q}(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

Source: GR (1.27) (PDF p. 42), EP (5.2.10) (p. 245). For \(F = \mathcal L\) this is the functional (8.91).

What is admissible? For \(F = \mathcal L\) we need \(\mathcal L\) and its partial derivatives to be continuous, that is, \(T\) and \(V\) must have continuous partial derivatives with respect to \(t\), \(\vek q\) and \(\dot{\vek q}\). The kinetic energy is a polynomial of second degree in the velocities, \(T = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M(t, \vek q)\,\dot{\vek q} + \vek b(t, \vek q)\cdot\dot{\vek q} + T_0\) (theorem 8.86), so this is true when \(\mat M\), \(\vek b\), \(T_0\) and \(V\) are continuously differentiable in \(t\) and \(\vek q\).

Theorem 8.102 Hamilton's principle (Hamiltonovo načelo)

Let a system have generalized coordinates \(\vek q\), ideal holonomic constraints solved in \(\vek q\) (definition 8.2), and kinetic energy and potential energy with continuous partial derivatives, as above. Let \(\vek q\) be a twice continuously differentiable function on \([t_1, t_2]\).

  1. If all applied forces are conservative, \(\vek q\) is a motion of the system, that is, it satisfies d'Alembert's principle (corollary 8.72), if and only if \(\vek q\) is a stationary point of the action \(\mathcal S\) among paths with the same end points \(\vek q(t_1)\), \(\vek q(t_2)\).
  2. If in addition to the conservative forces there are non-conservative ones with generalized forces \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}(t, \vek q, \dot{\vek q})\), continuous functions, \(\vek q\) is a motion if and only if for every admissible variation \(\vek\eta\)
    \[\delta\mathcal S(\vek q, \vek\eta) + \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \sum_{\mathrm{s}=1}^{n} Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}t = 0 . \tag{8.95}\]
Proof

We must show that the Euler-Lagrange equations of the action are exactly the Lagrange equations of section 8.9. Then the principle is another way of writing the same statement.

  1. The function \(F = \mathcal L\) has continuous partial derivatives. For a twice continuously differentiable \(\vek q\), \(\hat F_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}} = \partial T/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} M_{\mathrm{sk}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{k}} + b_{\mathrm{s}}\) is continuously differentiable: \(M_{\mathrm{sk}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{s}}\) are continuously differentiable functions of \(t\) and \(\vek q\), which is continuously differentiable, so by the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 1) they are continuously differentiable functions of \(t\), and \(\dot q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuously differentiable. The assumptions of theorem 8.98 are satisfied.
  2. By theorem 8.98, \(\vek q\) is a stationary point of the action if and only if \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) for every \(s\), that is,
    \[\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} - \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} = 0 .\]
  3. These are the Lagrange equations of a conservative system without non-conservative forces (theorem 8.90), which are by theorem 8.88 equivalent to d'Alembert's principle. This proves point 1.
  4. For point 2 take an admissible variation \(\vek\eta\). By equation (8.93), \(\delta\mathcal S(\vek q, \vek\eta) = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \sum_{\mathrm{s}} E_{\mathrm{s}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}t\) with \(E_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial\mathcal L/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\), so the left side of equation (8.95) equals \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \sum_{\mathrm{s}} (E_{\mathrm{s}} + Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}})\,\eta_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  5. If \(E_{\mathrm{s}} + Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\) for all \(s\), equation (8.95) holds for every \(\vek\eta\). If it holds for every \(\vek\eta\), we choose, as in step 5 of the proof of theorem 8.98, a variation that changes only one component, and from the fundamental lemma (lemma 4.77, the function \(E_{\mathrm{s}} + Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\) is continuous) we get \(E_{\mathrm{s}} + Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\), that is, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} - \partial\mathcal L/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\). These are the Lagrange equations with non-conservative forces (theorem 8.90).

Source: GR (1.27) (PDF p. 42, read), EP (5.2.8) (p. 244) for point 1, SHABANA (3.188) (PDF p. 149) for point 2. The proof is not from a source, the sources use the steps of integration by parts directly.

The idea of the theorem is that d'Alembert's principle at each instant, integrated over time, equals stationarity. Integration by parts in time moves the derivative from the inertial force \(m\,\ddot{\vek x}\) to the virtual displacement and turns the work of the inertial forces into a variation of the kinetic energy. This is step 3 of the proof of theorem 8.98. GR (PDF p. 41) therefore says that the principle is only the time-integrated form of the principle of virtual work.

Hamilton's principle thus does not give us a new equation of motion but the same one, in another way. The advantage is that the action is one number, independent of the coordinates: in whatever generalized coordinates we write it, we get the same equations. For pendulum A the action is \(\mathcal S = \int \big(\tfrac12\,m\,l^2\dot\theta^2 + m\,g\,l\cos\theta\big)\,\mathrm{d}t\) and theorem 8.98 gave \(\ddot\theta + (g/l)\sin\theta = 0\). The experiment from the beginning of the section is therefore a test of point 1: the derivative of the action with respect to \(\alpha\) was zero on the true path. With a non-conservative force, for example angular damping with the moment \(-c\,\dot\theta\), point 2 gives \(m\,l^2\ddot\theta + c\,\dot\theta + m\,g\,l\sin\theta = 0\), because \(Q^{\mathrm{nc}} = -c\,\dot\theta\).

The theorem says that the motion is a stationary point, not that it is the smallest value. The experiment showed this: at \(\tau = 0{,}5\) s the action on the true path is smaller than on the neighbouring paths, at \(\tau = 2\) s larger. The exact condition is shown by the second variation, which we will estimate later in this chapter in the section on buckling of a column.

8.10.4 The bar (palica)

So far the system had finitely many coordinates. The bar of chapters 3 and 7 has one coordinate for each cross section: the displacement \(u(x, t)\) of the cross section at the point \(x\) at time \(t\). Does the principle hold here too, and what does it give for the equation and the condition at the free end?

Take a bar of length \(L\) with constant \(A\), \(E\) and \(\rho\) (density), fixed at \(x = 0\), with the axis \(x\) along the bar. The load per unit length \(q(x, t)\) and the force \(F(t)\) at the end \(x = L\) point in the direction of increasing \(x\) and are continuous. The end has no mass and is free except for the force \(F\). All parts of the cross section move by \(u(x, t)\), so every point of the cross section at \(x\) has the velocity \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\). By definition 8.79 the kinetic energy of the bar is the integral with the density \(\rho\) over the volume \(A\,L\) of the bar, which by theorem 4.9 becomes an integral over \(x\) with the factor \(A\), \(T = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). The potential energy is the total potential energy of chapter 4 (equation (4.62)) at time \(t\), because the bar is linearly elastic: \(V = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q\,u\,\mathrm{d}x - F\,u(L, t)\). The action of the bar is therefore

\[\mathcal S(u) = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \bigg[\int_0^L \Big(\tfrac12\,\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{t}}^2 - \tfrac12\,EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + q\,u\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x + F(t)\,u(L, t)\bigg]\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{8.96}\]

The admissible functions are \(u\) on the rectangle \(\Omega = [0, L] \times [t_1, t_2]\) that have continuous \(u\), \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{tt}}\) there, satisfy \(u(0, t) = 0\) for every \(t\) and have prescribed displacements \(u(x, t_1)\) and \(u(x, t_2)\) (the positions of the bar at \(t_1\) and \(t_2\)). An admissible variation is a function \(\eta\) on \(\Omega\) with continuous \(\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{t}}\) (and hence continuous \(\eta\)) and \(\eta(0, t) = 0\), \(\eta(x, t_1) = \eta(x, t_2) = 0\). The first variation \(\delta\mathcal S(u, \eta)\) is the derivative of \(\mathcal S(u + \alpha\,\eta)\) with respect to \(\alpha\) at \(\alpha = 0\), as in definition 8.97.

Theorem 8.103 Hamilton's principle for a bar (Hamiltonovo načelo za palico)

Let \(u\) be an admissible function. Then \(u\) is a stationary point of the action (8.96) if and only if

\[\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{tt}} = EA\,u_{\mathrm{xx}} + q \quad \text{on } \Omega , \tag{8.97}\]

and at the free end for every \(t \in [t_1, t_2]\)

\[EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = F(t) . \tag{8.98}\]

Equation (8.98) is called the dynamic boundary condition (dinamični robni pogoj).

Proof

We must show that the first variation is the sum of an integral over the rectangle and an integral over the end of the bar. Then we separate the equation with bumps, and the condition with a variation that is not zero at the end.

  1. The integrand in (8.96) at \(u + \alpha\,\eta\) is a polynomial of second degree in \(\alpha\) with coefficients that are continuous functions on \(\Omega\). Hence \(\mathcal S(u + \alpha\,\eta) = \mathcal S(u) + \alpha\,B_1 + \alpha^2 B_2\) with
    \[B_1 = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2}\!\!\int_0^L \big(\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{t}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{t}} - EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{x}} + q\,\eta\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t + \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} F\,\eta(L, t)\,\mathrm{d}t ,\]
    \[B_2 = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2}\!\!\int_0^L \Big(\tfrac12\,\rho A\,\eta_{\mathrm{t}}^2 - \tfrac12\,EA\,\eta_{\mathrm{x}}^2\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
    The integrals exist, because the integrands are continuous (theorem 3.38), and the splitting follows from the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.39). The derivative with respect to \(\alpha\) at \(0\) is \(\delta\mathcal S(u, \eta) = B_1\). Equations (8.97) and (8.98) will follow from \(B_1 = 0\).
  2. For every \(x\), \(\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{t}}(x, \cdot)\) and \(\eta(x, \cdot)\) are continuously differentiable functions of \(t\) (continuous \(u_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{t}}\)). Integration by parts (corollary 3.41) gives \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \rho A\,u_{\mathrm{t}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t = \big[\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{t}}\,\eta\big]_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} - \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \rho A\,u_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\eta\,\mathrm{d}t\), and the term in the square bracket is zero, because \(\eta(x, t_1) = \eta(x, t_2) = 0\). We may exchange the order of integration (theorem 4.9, the version for a rectangle), so the first term in \(B_1\) equals \(-\int\!\int \rho A\,u_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\eta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  3. For every \(t\), \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(\cdot, t)\) and \(\eta(\cdot, t)\) are continuously differentiable functions of \(x\) (continuous \(u_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\)). Integration by parts gives \(-\int_0^L EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)\,\eta(L, t) + \int_0^L EA\,u_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\eta\,\mathrm{d}x\), where the term at \(x = 0\) drops out because \(\eta(0, t) = 0\).
  4. Substituting steps 2 and 3 into \(B_1\) we obtain for every admissible variation
    \[\begin{aligned} \delta\mathcal S(u, \eta) &= \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2}\!\!\int_0^L R\,\eta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &\quad + \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \big(F(t) - EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)\big)\,\eta(L, t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \end{aligned} \tag{8.99}\]
    where \(R = -\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{tt}} + EA\,u_{\mathrm{xx}} + q\) is a continuous function on \(\Omega\).
  5. If (8.97) and (8.98) hold, \(R = 0\) and \(F - EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\), so by step 4 \(\delta\mathcal S(u, \eta) = 0\) for every admissible variation. The function \(u\) is a stationary point.
  6. Conversely, let \(u\) be a stationary point. For numbers \(0 < \alpha_1 < \beta_1 < L\) and \(t_1 < \alpha_2 < \beta_2 < t_2\) let \(\eta(x, t) = p_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,p_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(t)\) (lemma 4.83, point 1). It has continuous \(\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{t}}\), is zero at \(x = 0\), \(x = L\), \(t = t_1\) and \(t = t_2\), so it is an admissible variation with \(\eta(L, t) = 0\). By step 4, \(\int\!\int R\,\eta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\). Since \(\eta\) is zero outside \([\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2]\), this is an integral over this rectangle, and by theorem 4.9 we may write it with the inner integral over \(t\). For all such \(\alpha_1, \beta_1, \alpha_2, \beta_2\) the assumption of point 3 of lemma 4.83 holds for the rectangle \(\Omega\) with coordinates \(x\) and \(y = t\) and the continuous function \(f(x, y) = R(x, y)\), so \(R = 0\) on \(\Omega\). This is equation (8.97).
  7. Let \(\psi\) be a function with a continuous derivative on \([t_1, t_2]\) and \(\psi(t_1) = \psi(t_2) = 0\), and \(\eta(x, t) = (x/L)\,\psi(t)\). It has continuous \(\eta_{\mathrm{x}} = \psi/L\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{t}} = (x/L)\,\dot\psi\), is zero at \(x = 0\), \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), so it is admissible, and \(\eta(L, t) = \psi(t)\). By step 6 the first integral in (8.99) is zero, so \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \big(F - EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)\big)\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\). The function \(F - EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, \cdot)\) is continuous, and by the fundamental lemma (lemma 4.77) it is zero on \([t_1, t_2]\). This is (8.98).

Source: EP example 5.3.1 (pp. 251 to 252), CM §7.7.3 (7.7.30) (PDF p. 367). The sources derive the equations from \(\delta\mathcal S = 0\) by integration by parts and the conclusion that the coefficients are zero, without determining which variations are admissible. The proof in steps is not from a source.

Equation (8.97) is the equilibrium of a slice of the bar (section 4.4.4) to which the inertial force \(-\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{tt}}\) is added (section 8.7): \(N_{\mathrm{x}} + q = \rho A\,u_{\mathrm{tt}}\) for the axial force \(N = EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}\). The dynamic boundary condition is the natural boundary condition of theorem 5.69, now at every instant, not only at rest: the force in the bar at \(x = L\) at time \(t\) equals the force \(F(t)\) acting on the end. We did not prescribe the condition. The action is sensitive to it only because the displacement at \(x = L\) is not prescribed, and so the principle chooses it by itself (figure 8.32). At \(x = 0\) we prescribe the displacement, so there is no natural condition.

Let us test it on the hanging bar of chapters 4 to 7. A steel bar, \(L = 10\) m, diameter 10 mm, \(A = 78{,}54\) mm², \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³, axis \(x\) pointing down, fixed at \(x = 0\), lower end free, \(F = 0\). Its only load is its weight, \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m. The bar rests in the equilibrium position \(u_{\mathrm{s}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952\cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^{-1}\), and the lower end is displaced by \(u_{\mathrm{s}}(L) = a\,L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm. This position satisfies (8.97), since \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = 0\) and \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{s}}'' + q = -2aEA + \rho g A = 0\), and (8.98), since \(u_{\mathrm{s}}'(L) = 2a\,(L - L) = 0 = F/EA\). The motion we study is a departure from this position.

Let us look at the first variation in the window \(t_1 = 0\), \(t_2 = 10\) ms, with the variation \(\eta = (x/L)\,\psi(t)\), where \(\psi(t) = 16\,t^2\,(t_2 - t)^2/t_2^4\) is a dimensionless function with maximum value \(1\) (in what follows \(\alpha\) is in metres). The end of the bar thus has the value \(\psi\) in \(\eta\), which is exactly the variation that in step 7 of the proof touches the dynamic condition. By formula (8.99), \(\delta\mathcal S(u_{\mathrm{s}}, \eta) = 0\) (SymPy: \(10^{-16}\) N s, which is rounding). Now try the field \(u_{\mathrm{s}} + c\,x\) with \(c = 10^{-6}\). It satisfies equation (8.97) (the term \(c\,x\) is linear in \(x\) and constant in time), but not the condition: \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{x}}(L) = EA\,c = 15{,}39\) N instead of \(0\). The first variation is \(\delta\mathcal S = -EA\,c\int_0^{t_2}\psi\,\mathrm{d}t = -15{,}39\ \text{N}\cdot 5{,}333\ \text{ms} = -0{,}0821\) N s, which agrees with the SymPy computation. The field would be a motion only for a bar with a force \(F = 15{,}39\) N at the end. Without it, it is not stationary: the condition at the end is not an unnecessary addition but the content of the principle.

Now the second variation. For \(\eta = (x/L)\,\psi\) we have \(B_2 = \tfrac12\,\rho A\,\tfrac{L}{3}\int\dot\psi^2\,\mathrm{d}t - \tfrac12\,\tfrac{EA}{L}\int\psi^2\,\mathrm{d}t\). For our \(\psi\), \(\int\dot\psi^2/\int\psi^2 = 12/\tau^2\) on a window of length \(\tau = t_2 - t_1\), so \(B_2 > 0\) if and only if \(\tau < 2L\sqrt{\rho/E} = 3{,}990\) ms, which follows from \(\rho L^2/(3E) \cdot 12/\tau^2 > 1\). At \(\tau = 1\) ms \(B_2 = +4666\) N s/m, at \(\tau = 10\) ms \(B_2 = -2630\) N s/m. For this variation the action therefore increases in \(\alpha^2\) for a short window and decreases for a longer one. For the longer window the stationary position is thus not the smallest action, as for the pendulum. For the short window we tested only one variation. The frequencies of the bar and the solution of equation (8.97) belong to chapter 13.

Hamilton's principle thus gave, for the pendulum, for a system with kinetic energy and for the bar, the same structure: stationarity of the action means equations in the interior and natural conditions where the displacement is not prescribed. For a system of points this structure is theorem 8.102, for the bar theorem 8.103. Both times the action is stationary, not the smallest. The equations of motion obtained are the same as in section 8.9, so we look at what follows from them: section 8.11 finds out why the pendulum conserves energy and which numbers remain constant.

8.11 Conservation laws (Ohranitveni zakoni)

For the pendulum of section 8.9 we solved the equation of motion \(\ddot\theta + \tfrac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta = 0\) numerically with RK4 (Runge-Kutta of fourth order, metoda RK4) and after every step computed the sum of the kinetic and the potential energy. In 10 s and 20 000 steps the sum changed by \(4{,}6 \cdot 10^{-13}\) J. This change is an error of the computation and not a property of the motion, since RK4 does not conserve energy exactly: with 10 000 steps it is \(6{,}5 \cdot 10^{-12}\) J, with 20 000 steps \(4{,}6 \cdot 10^{-13}\) J and with 40 000 steps \(4{,}0 \cdot 10^{-13}\) J, where it is already limited by the round-off error of the computer. The equation of motion itself conserves energy exactly. Why does the energy stay constant, and which numbers stay constant in other systems described by Lagrange's equations?

The state of a system with \(n\) generalized coordinates (posplošene koordinate) at time \(t\) is the \(n\) coordinates \(\vek q\) and the \(n\) velocities \(\dot{\vek q}\). A motion is a curve \(\vek q(t)\) and at each of its points we can compute many numbers from the state. We are interested in those that do not change along any motion. If we know them, we know something about the motion without solving the equations. For the pendulum, for example, the height from which we released it gives the speed at the lowest position.

Definition 8.104 Conserved quantity (ohranjena količina)

Let \(F(t, \vek q, \dot{\vek q})\) be a continuously differentiable function that assigns a number to the state of a system with \(n\) generalized coordinates at time \(t\). The function \(F\) is a conserved quantity of the system if for every motion \(\vek q(t)\) that solves the equations of motion of the system on an interval \(I\), the number \(F(t, \vek q(t), \dot{\vek q}(t))\) is the same for all \(t \in I\).

8.11.1 Energy (Energija)

For a system whose constraints do not contain time, the kinetic energy is by theorem 8.86 a quadratic form of the velocities, \(T = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T \mat M(\vek q)\,\dot{\vek q}\) with a symmetric mass matrix \(\mat M\). For the pendulum \(T = \tfrac12 m\ell^2\dot\theta^2\). Differentiating with respect to the velocity gives \(m\ell^2\dot\theta\), and multiplying by the velocity \(\dot\theta\) gives \(m\ell^2\dot\theta^2 = 2T\). The factor \(\tfrac12\) in \(T\) and the factor 2 from differentiating the square cancel, and multiplying by the velocity restores the power, so \(2T\) remains and not \(T\). The same computation holds for all such systems.

Lemma 8.105 Euler's identity for the kinetic energy (Eulerjeva enakost za kinetično energijo)

Let \(T(\vek q, \dot{\vek q}) = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T \mat M(\vek q)\,\dot{\vek q}\), where \(\mat M(\vek q)\) is a symmetric \(n \times n\) matrix of numbers that does not depend on \(\dot{\vek q}\). Then for every state \((\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\)

\[\sum_{\mathrm{s}=1}^{n} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = 2\,T . \tag{8.100}\]
Proof

We must show that the derivative with respect to the velocities, multiplied by the velocities, gives twice the quadratic form.

  1. Write \(T = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{a},\mathrm{b}} M_{\mathrm{ab}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{a}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{b}}\), where \(M_{\mathrm{ab}}\) does not depend on the velocities.
  2. The derivative \(\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{a}}/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is \(1\) for \(a = s\) and \(0\) otherwise. By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.81, sum and product) we get \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}}\big(\dot q_{\mathrm{a}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{b}}\big) = \delta_{\mathrm{as}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{b}} + \dot q_{\mathrm{a}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{bs}}\), where \(\delta_{\mathrm{as}} = 1\) for \(a = s\) and \(0\) otherwise. For \(a = b = s\) this gives \(2\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\), as it must for \(\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). Hence \(\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = \tfrac12 \Big( \sum_{\mathrm{b}} M_{\mathrm{sb}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{b}} + \sum_{\mathrm{a}} M_{\mathrm{as}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{a}} \Big)\).
  3. The matrix is symmetric, \(M_{\mathrm{as}} = M_{\mathrm{sa}}\), so the two sums are equal and \(\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{b}} M_{\mathrm{sb}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{b}}\).
  4. Multiply by \(\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) and sum over \(s\): \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}} \sum_{\mathrm{b}} M_{\mathrm{sb}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{b}} = \dot{\vek q}^\T \mat M\,\dot{\vek q} = 2T\). This is (8.100).

Source: GR (1.34) (PDF p. 46), which obtains it from Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions (1.35) for degree 2. The proof for a quadratic form is not from the source.

The lemma showed that for a quadratic kinetic energy there is a relation between the derivative and the value that we need for the energy law. We still have to say which forces we allow. Conservative forces with a potential \(V(\vek q)\) (definition 8.53) enter the function \(\mathcal{L} = T - V\). All other generalized forces we collect in \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\) (non-conservative forces, nekonservativne sile), as in theorem 8.90. Their power is \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) by definition 8.54, and by lemma 8.55 it is the derivative of their work. Viscous damping, which opposes the velocity, is such a force. Non-conservative forces are dissipative (disipativne) if their power is \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} \le 0\) in every state, that is, together they never do positive work. GR (PDF p. 52) takes the narrower case of a force parallel to the velocity and opposite to it, which satisfies this condition. We call the sum \(\mathcal{E} = T + V\) the total mechanical energy (celotna mehanska energija).

Theorem 8.106 Conservation of energy of a system (ohranitev energije)

Let a system have \(n\) degrees of freedom, ideal scleronomic holonomic constraints (definition 8.42), conservative forces with a potential \(V(\vek q)\) that does not depend on time, and possibly other generalized forces \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\). Let \(\vek q(t)\) be a twice continuously differentiable motion that solves the equations of theorem 8.90. Then \(\mathcal{E}(t) = T + V\) is continuously differentiable and

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}=1}^{n} Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} . \tag{8.101}\]

If all \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\), then \(\mathcal{E}\) is a conserved quantity (definition 8.104). If the forces are dissipative, \(\mathcal{E}\) does not increase with time.

Proof

We must show that \(\mathcal{E}\) changes only by the power of the forces that we did not include in the potential.

  1. Scleronomic means \(\vek X = \vek X(\vek q)\) without time, so \(T = \tfrac12 \dot{\vek q}^\T \mat M(\vek q)\,\dot{\vek q}\) (theorem 8.86) and \(\mathcal{L} = T - V\) does not contain \(t\). The motion solves \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} + Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\) (theorem 8.90).
  2. By the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 1) \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}}\,\ddot q_{\mathrm{s}}\). There is no term with \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial t\), because \(\mathcal{L}\) does not contain time.
  3. By the product rule (lemma 1.81) \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \ddot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}}\).
  4. Subtract step 2 from step 3. The terms with \(\ddot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) cancel and by step 1 we are left with \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Big( \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} - \mathcal{L} \Big) = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}} \Big( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} - \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} \Big) = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\).
  5. \(V\) does not contain the velocities, so \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial T/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) and by lemma 8.105 \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} = 2T\). The expression in the brackets of step 4 is therefore \(2T - (T - V) = T + V = \mathcal{E}\). This is (8.101).
  6. If all \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\), then \(\mathcal{E}' = 0\) on the whole interval and by corollary 1.85 \(\mathcal{E}(t)\) is the same for all \(t\). If \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} \le 0\), then for \(t_1 < t_2\) by theorem 1.84 \(\mathcal{E}(t_2) - \mathcal{E}(t_1) = \mathcal{E}'(\xi)\,(t_2 - t_1) \le 0\) for some \(\xi \in (t_1, t_2)\), so \(\mathcal{E}\) does not increase.

Source: GR (1.42) to (1.46) (PDF pp. 47 to 48, conservation of energy for scleronomic constraints and conservative forces), (1.55) (PDF p. 53, energy for dissipative forces) and (1.58) (PDF p. 54, derivative of the energy with non-conservative forces). GR derives it from Lagrange's equations along the same path, the notation with the function \(\mathcal{L}\) and steps 2 to 4 are ours.

The proof showed that \(\mathcal{E}\) changes only because of forces that do not come from a potential, and that the key is lemma 8.105: for a quadratic kinetic energy the expression \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}} - \mathcal{L}\) is exactly \(T + V\). In step 2 we also see where the energy law comes from. If \(\mathcal{L}\) contained time, a term \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial t\) would appear there and in step 4 an extra term \(-\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial t\) would remain.

Example 8.107 Pendulum: speed from the energy and loss by damping (nihalo: hitrost iz energije in izguba pri dušenju)

The pendulum of example A: a point mass \(m = 1\) kg on a rigid light rod of length \(\ell = 1\) m, angle \(\theta\) from the vertical downward, \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s\(^2\). The potential is \(V = -mg\ell\cos\theta\), the kinetic energy \(T = \tfrac12 m\ell^2\dot\theta^2\).

  1. Release it from rest at \(\theta = 90^\circ\). Then \(T = 0\) and \(V = -mg\ell\cos 90^\circ = 0\), so \(\mathcal{E} = 0\) J.
  2. At the lowest position \(\theta = 0\) we have \(V = -mg\ell = -9{,}81\) J. Since \(\mathcal{E}\) is constant, \(T = 9{,}81\) J, so \(\tfrac12 m\ell^2\dot\theta^2 = 9{,}81\) J and \(|\dot\theta| = \sqrt{2g/\ell} = 4{,}4294\) 1/s. The speed of the mass is \(\ell\,|\dot\theta| = 4{,}43\) m/s.
  3. At \(\theta = 45^\circ\) we have \(T = \mathcal{E} - V = mg\ell\cos 45^\circ\), so \(|\dot\theta| = \sqrt{2g\cos 45^\circ/\ell} = 3{,}7247\) 1/s. We obtained the speed at the intermediate position without the equation of motion.
  4. Release it from rest at \(10^\circ\) and at \(170^\circ\). Then \(\mathcal{E} = -9{,}661\) J and \(+9{,}661\) J, and the speeds at the lowest position are \(0{,}5460\) 1/s and \(6{,}2403\) 1/s. A higher starting position means more energy and therefore a larger speed at the same position.

Let us add a damping moment \(Q^{\mathrm{nc}} = -c\,\dot\theta\) with \(c = 0{,}2\) N m s at the hinge. The power is \(Q^{\mathrm{nc}}\,\dot\theta = -c\,\dot\theta^2 \le 0\), the force is dissipative, and by (8.101) \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}/\mathrm{d}t = -c\,\dot\theta^2\). The numerical RK4 solution from \(90^\circ\) gives \(\mathcal{E} = -1{,}869\) J after 1 s, \(-3{,}279\) J after 2 s, \(-6{,}016\) J after 5 s and \(-8{,}348\) J after 10 s. The energy therefore decreases and approaches \(-9{,}81\) J, the value for rest at the lowest position. The loss in 10 s is \(\mathcal{E}(0) - \mathcal{E}(10) = 8{,}3477\) J, and the integral \(\int_0^{10} c\,\dot\theta^2\,\mathrm{d}t\) along the solution is also \(8{,}3477\) J, as the time integral of (8.101) requires.

Example 8.108 Toggle mechanism: the velocity-square term (kolenasti mehanizem: člen s kvadratom hitrosti)

Mechanism D (two bars, a slider, a spring and a load \(P = 100\) N at the joint) has \(T = \tfrac12 m(\theta)\,\dot\theta^2\) with \(m(\theta) = \tfrac13 + 2\sin^2\theta\) kg m\(^2\) and the potential \(V(\theta)\) from section 8.5. The equation of motion is \(m(\theta)\,\ddot\theta + \tfrac12 m'(\theta)\,\dot\theta^2 + V'(\theta) = 0\) (section 8.9). We check the conservation of \(\mathcal{E}\) and see what happens if we omit the velocity-square term.

  1. By the product rule and the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 3) \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(\tfrac12 m(\theta)\,\dot\theta^2\big) = m\,\dot\theta\,\ddot\theta + \tfrac12 m'\,\dot\theta^3\), since in differentiation \(m(\theta(t))\) also changes with time. So \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot\theta\,\big( m\,\ddot\theta + \tfrac12 m'\,\dot\theta^2 + V' \big)\) and the bracket is the equation of motion, hence zero.
  2. Release the mechanism from rest at \(\theta = 0{,}7\) rad. There \(\mathcal{E} = V = 83{,}401\) J. The equilibrium position \(0{,}50523\) rad has \(V = 24{,}609\) J and \(m = 0{,}80185\) kg m\(^2\), so \(T = 83{,}401 - 24{,}609 = 58{,}792\) J and \(|\dot\theta| = \sqrt{2T/m} = 12{,}110\) 1/s.
  3. The other turning point, where \(\dot\theta = 0\) and again \(V(\theta) = 83{,}401\) J, is at \(0{,}14547\) rad. The unstable position at \(2{,}15^\circ = 0{,}0375\) rad lies to the left of it, so the mechanism does not reach it.
  4. RK4 after 3 s with 30 000 steps: \(\mathcal{E}\) changes by \(1{,}7 \cdot 10^{-9}\) J. If we omit the term \(\tfrac12 m'\,\dot\theta^2\), the computed energy changes by 25,5 J, because \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}/\mathrm{d}t\) from step 1 is no longer zero. The velocity-square term is therefore part of the law and must not be dropped.

In the proof of theorem 8.106 we used that the constraints do not contain time. What remains if a constraint moves? For a rheonomic constraint the kinetic energy by theorem 8.86 has three parts, \(T = T_2 + T_1 + T_0\): \(T_2 = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}\) is a quadratic form of the velocities, \(T_1 = \vek b\cdot\dot{\vek q}\) is linear and \(T_0\) does not contain the velocities. Lemma 8.105 holds only for \(T_2\): for \(T_1\) we have \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial T_1/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} = T_1\) and for \(T_0\) the sum is zero. So the conserved quantity changes too, as the next theorem shows. Its proof repeats steps 1 to 4 of the previous one.

Theorem 8.109 Energy integral for rheonomic constraints (energijski integral pri reonomnih vezeh)

Let \(\vek q(t)\) be a twice continuously differentiable motion of a system with ideal holonomic constraints that solves the equations of theorem 8.90 with \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\). Let \(\mat M\), \(\vek b\), \(T_0\) from theorem 8.86 and \(V\) not contain the time \(t\). Then

\[\mathcal{E}^* = T_2 - T_0 + V \tag{8.102}\]

is a conserved quantity (definition 8.104).

Proof

We must show that \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} - \mathcal{L}\) is constant and equal to \(\mathcal{E}^*\).

  1. \(\mathcal{L} = T - V = T_2 + T_1 + T_0 - V\) does not contain \(t\), so by the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 1), as in step 2 of the previous proof, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}}\,\ddot q_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  2. By the product rule (lemma 1.81), as in step 3, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \ddot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}}\).
  3. Subtract the first from the second. By theorem 8.90 with \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\) we have \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\), so \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Big( \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} - \mathcal{L} \Big) = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}} \Big( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} - \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} \Big) = 0\).
  4. \(V\) does not contain the velocities, so \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial (T_2 + T_1)/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) (\(T_0\) does not contain the velocities). For \(T_2\) the sum is \(2T_2\) by lemma 8.105, for \(T_1 = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} b_{\mathrm{s}}(\vek q)\,\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\) it is \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\,b_{\mathrm{s}} = T_1\).
  5. So the expression in the brackets of step 3 equals \(2T_2 + T_1 - (T_2 + T_1 + T_0 - V) = T_2 - T_0 + V = \mathcal{E}^*\). By corollary 1.85 \(\mathcal{E}^*(t)\) is the same for all \(t\).

Source: Not from the source in this form: GR (1.46) (PDF p. 48) writes the energy integral for scleronomic constraints, where \(T_1 = T_0 = 0\). For rheonomic constraints GR (PDF p. 54) uses the potential \(V^* = V - T_0\) (by the text of the page), which agrees with \(\mathcal{E}^*\). The proof is ours.

This energy integral (energijski integral) differs from \(T + V\), which now changes. The difference \(\mathcal{E}^* - (T + V) = -2T_0 - T_1\) is zero when the constraints are scleronomic.

Example 8.110 Ring on a rotating rod (obroč na vrteči se palici)

A ring of mass \(m = 0{,}1\) kg slides without friction on a straight rod in a horizontal plane. The rod rotates about one of its points with constant angular velocity \(\Omega = 2\) 1/s, gravity does not act in the plane. This is our model. The coordinate is the distance \(r\) of the ring from the pivot. The position of the ring is \((r\cos\Omega t,\ r\sin\Omega t)\) and the constraint is rheonomic. The velocity of the ring has the components \((\dot r\cos\Omega t - r\Omega\sin\Omega t,\ \dot r\sin\Omega t + r\Omega\cos\Omega t)\), its square is \(\dot r^2 + r^2\Omega^2\). So \(T_2 = \tfrac12 m\,\dot r^2\), \(T_1 = 0\) and \(T_0 = \tfrac12 m\,\Omega^2 r^2\), there is no potential and \(\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12 m\,(\dot r^2 + \Omega^2 r^2)\) does not contain \(t\). Lagrange's equation is \(m\,\ddot r = m\,\Omega^2 r\) (SymPy).

  1. By theorem 8.109 \(\mathcal{E}^* = T_2 - T_0 = \tfrac12 m\,(\dot r^2 - \Omega^2 r^2)\) is conserved. If we release the ring at \(r = 0{,}5\) m with \(\dot r = 0\), its value is \(-\tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}1 \cdot 4 \cdot 0{,}25 = -0{,}05\) J.
  2. From \(\tfrac12 m\,(\dot r^2 - \Omega^2 r^2) = -0{,}05\) J we get \(\dot r^2 = \Omega^2 r^2 - 2 \cdot 0{,}05/m\). At \(r = 1\) m this is \(4 - 1 = 3\) m\(^2\)/s\(^2\), so \(\dot r = 1{,}7321\) m/s.
  3. Then \(T + V = T = \tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}1 \cdot (3 + 4) = 0{,}35\) J, and at the start \(\tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}1 \cdot (0 + 4 \cdot 0{,}25) = 0{,}05\) J. The sum \(T + V\) grew by 0,30 J. The rod pushes the ring in the direction of rotation and does work in the actual displacement, because it moves itself. The constraint is nevertheless ideal: in a virtual displacement with frozen time (section 8.4) its force does no work, since it is perpendicular to the rod and the displacement is along it. So there is no generalized constraint force in Lagrange's equation, but in the energy \(T + V\) there is its work.

Finally let us see what the conservation of energy says about the motion of the pendulum. The state of the pendulum is a pair \((\theta, \dot\theta)\) in the plane and a motion is a curve in this plane. Since \(\mathcal{E}\) is constant, every motion lies on a level curve (nivojnica) of the function \(\mathcal{E}(\theta, \dot\theta) = \tfrac12 m\ell^2\dot\theta^2 - mg\ell\cos\theta\), that is, on the curve with the equation

\[\dot\theta = \pm\sqrt{\frac{2\,(\mathcal{E} + mg\ell\cos\theta)}{m\ell^2}} , \tag{8.103}\]

which is real only where \(\mathcal{E} + mg\ell\cos\theta \ge 0\). For the pendulum the motion is unique for a given state (corollary 8.94), so the level curves do not cross, except at the resting positions, where \(\dot\theta = 0\) and the motion is constant. Figure 8.33 shows the level curves for \(m = 1\) kg and \(\ell = 1\) m.

From equation (8.103) we read three regions. Since \(T \ge 0\), we have \(\mathcal{E} \ge V \ge -mg\ell\) and the value \(-mg\ell = -9{,}81\) J belongs only to rest at the lowest position (the centre of the curves in the figure). For \(-mg\ell < \mathcal{E} < mg\ell\) we have \(\cos\theta \ge -\mathcal{E}/(mg\ell)\) and this is the interval \(|\theta| \le \theta_{\max}\), where \(0 < \theta_{\max} < \pi\) and \(\cos\theta_{\max} = -\mathcal{E}/(mg\ell)\). The speed is zero at the end points and has both signs in between, so the level curve is a closed curve and the pendulum oscillates between \(-\theta_{\max}\) and \(\theta_{\max}\). For \(\mathcal{E} = 0\) we have \(\theta_{\max} = 90^\circ\), which is our release. For \(\mathcal{E} = mg\ell\) the double-angle formula \(1 + \cos\theta = 2\cos^2(\theta/2)\) gives \(\dot\theta = \pm 2\sqrt{g/\ell}\,\cos(\theta/2)\) for \(|\theta| \le \pi\), and at \(\theta = 0\) it is \(2\sqrt{g/\ell} = 6{,}2642\) 1/s. This curve ends at \((\pm\pi, 0)\), which is the state of rest of the unstable equilibrium position (section 8.6). For \(\mathcal{E} > mg\ell\) we have \(\mathcal{E} + mg\ell\cos\theta > 0\) for every \(\theta\), the speed is never zero and keeps its sign, and the pendulum rotates. At \(\mathcal{E} = 15\) J the value \(|\dot\theta|\) is smallest at the top position, \(\sqrt{2\,(15 - 9{,}81)} = 3{,}2218\) 1/s, and largest at the bottom, \(7{,}0441\) 1/s. The figure shows where oscillation turns into rotation: at the energy that is just enough for the pendulum to reach the top position. There the speed decreases towards zero, so the motion near this energy is slow and the oscillation period gets longer: for an amplitude of \(170^\circ\) it is \(4{,}8935\) s, 2,44 times longer than the \(2{,}0061\) s for a small amplitude (section 8.9).

8.11.2 Cyclic coordinates and generalized momentum (Ciklične koordinate in posplošena gibalna količina)

Energy is one conserved quantity, which belongs to an \(\mathcal{L}\) without time. Are there others? Take a free point of mass \(m\) in the plane \((x, y)\) with no forces in the direction of the \(x\) axis. Its equation of motion in the \(x\) direction is \(m\,\ddot x = 0\) and \(m\,\dot x\) is constant. In Lagrange's form \(\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12 m\,(\dot x^2 + \dot y^2) - V(y)\), which does not contain \(x\), and the equation for \(x\) is \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot x} = 0\). The same structure holds for every coordinate that \(\mathcal{L}\) does not contain.

Definition 8.111 Generalized momentum (posplošena gibalna količina)

Let \(\mathcal{L}(t, \vek q, \dot{\vek q}) = T - V\) be the Lagrangian of a system with \(n\) generalized coordinates. The generalized momentum belonging to the coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the function of the state

\[p_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} , \qquad s = 1, \dots, n . \tag{8.104}\]

Since \(V\) does not contain the velocities, \(p_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial T/\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}\). For scleronomic constraints, by step 3 of the proof of lemma 8.105, \(p_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{b}} M_{\mathrm{sb}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{b}}\). A coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) that \(\mathcal{L}\) does not contain (that is, \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) in every state) is cyclic (ciklična).

The unit of \(p_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the unit of the generalized force multiplied by a second: kg m/s if \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is a length and N m s if \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is an angle. For the free point from the introduction \(p_{\mathrm{x}} = m\,\dot x\), which is the momentum (gibalna količina) in the \(x\) direction. For the pendulum \(p_\theta = m\ell^2\dot\theta\), which is the angular momentum (kotna količina) of the mass about the pivot: the mass has the velocity \(\ell\dot\theta\) perpendicular to the rod, and the distance \(\ell\) multiplies \(m\,\ell\dot\theta\).

Corollary 8.112 A cyclic coordinate gives a conserved quantity (ciklična koordinata da ohranjeno količino)

Let \(\vek q(t)\) be a motion from theorem 8.90 and let \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) be a cyclic coordinate, \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\). Then \(p_{\mathrm{s}}\) is a conserved quantity.

Proof

We must show that the time derivative of \(p_{\mathrm{s}}\) is zero.

  1. The equation for \(s\) from theorem 8.90 is \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot q_{\mathrm{s}}} = \dfrac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} + Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}}\), which is \(\dot p_{\mathrm{s}}\) by (8.104).
  2. The right-hand side is zero: \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\), because the coordinate is cyclic, and \(Q_{\mathrm{s}}^{\mathrm{nc}} = 0\).
  3. So \(\dot p_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) on the whole interval and by corollary 1.85 \(p_{\mathrm{s}}\) is constant.

Source: Not from a source: no book of the project has a cyclic coordinate (search in GR, SHABANA, CK, EP, CM, SPONG), the equation is Lagrange's equation from theorem 8.90.

The momentum and angular momentum of a free system we obtain as cases of a cyclic coordinate. Take \(N\) points with masses \(m_{\mathrm{i}}\) and positions \(\vek r_{\mathrm{i}}\) in the plane, whose only forces are internal forces from a potential \(V\) that depends only on the distances \(|\vek r_{\mathrm{i}} - \vek r_{\mathrm{j}}|\). If we shift all points by \(a\) in the direction of the \(x\) axis, this is the coordinate \(q_1 = a\), and the remaining coordinates describe the positions of the points relative to this shifted picture, then the distances between the points are the same, so \(V\) does not contain \(a\). Neither does \(T\) contain \(a\), since the velocities do not change if all points are shifted by the same distance. The coordinate \(a\) is therefore cyclic and \(p_{\mathrm{a}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} m_{\mathrm{i}}\,\dot x_{\mathrm{i}}\), because each \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) contains \(a\) with derivative 1. This is the \(x\) component of the total momentum. For a rotation of all points by an angle \(\varphi\) about the origin, \(\vek r_{\mathrm{i}} = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{i}})\) changes with \(\partial \vek r_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial\varphi = (-y_{\mathrm{i}}, x_{\mathrm{i}})\), the distances and speeds do not change, so \(\varphi\) is cyclic and \(p_\varphi = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} m_{\mathrm{i}}\,(-\dot x_{\mathrm{i}}\,y_{\mathrm{i}} + \dot y_{\mathrm{i}}\,x_{\mathrm{i}})\). By (2.32) this is the \(z\) component of the vector \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \vek r_{\mathrm{i}} \times m_{\mathrm{i}}\dot{\vek r}_{\mathrm{i}}\), the angular momentum of the system about the origin. The conservation of momentum and angular momentum of a free system is therefore a special case of corollary 8.112: each belongs to one kind of displacement that \(\mathcal{L}\) does not detect. Energy belongs to a displacement in time. The same is shown by step 2 of the proof of theorem 8.106: \(\mathcal{E}\) is conserved because \(\mathcal{L}\) does not contain \(t\).

Example 8.113 Free bar in the plane (prosta palica v ravnini)

The uniform bar of example C (\(L = 2\) m, \(m = 30\) kg, \(J_{\mathrm{G}} = mL^2/12 = 10\) kg m\(^2\)) flies freely in a vertical plane, without constraints, under its weight. This is our model. The coordinates are \(x\) and \(y\) of the centre of mass \(G\) (\(y\) axis upward) and the angle \(\varphi\) of the bar. By theorem 8.82 for planar motion \(T = \tfrac12 m\,(\dot x^2 + \dot y^2) + \tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{G}}\dot\varphi^2\), the potential of the weight is \(V = mg\,y\), so

\[\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12 m\,(\dot x^2 + \dot y^2) + \tfrac12 J_{\mathrm{G}}\,\dot\varphi^2 - mg\,y . \tag{8.105}\]

The coordinates \(x\) and \(\varphi\) are cyclic, \(y\) is not.

  1. The generalized momenta by (8.104): \(p_{\mathrm{x}} = m\,\dot x\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}} = m\,\dot y\), \(p_\varphi = J_{\mathrm{G}}\,\dot\varphi\). By corollary 8.112 \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(p_\varphi\) are constant and \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) is not: \(\dot p_{\mathrm{y}} = -mg\) from the equation for \(y\).
  2. We throw the bar from \(y = 0\) with velocity \((\dot x, \dot y) = (2, 5)\) m/s and angular velocity \(\dot\varphi = 3\) 1/s. Then \(p_{\mathrm{x}} = 30 \cdot 2 = 60\) kg m/s, \(p_\varphi = 10 \cdot 3 = 30\) kg m\(^2\)/s and \(p_{\mathrm{y}} = 30 \cdot 5 = 150\) kg m/s. The energy is \(\mathcal{E} = \tfrac12 \cdot 30 \cdot (4 + 25) + \tfrac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 + 0 = 480\) J.
  3. At the highest position \(\dot y = 0\), and \(\dot x = 2\), \(\dot\varphi = 3\) remain by step 1. Then \(\mathcal{E} = 480 = \tfrac12 \cdot 30 \cdot 4 + \tfrac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 + mg\,h = 105 + 294{,}3\,h\), so \(h = 1{,}2742\) m. This is the same as \(\dot y_0^2/(2g) = 25/19{,}62 = 1{,}2742\) m, the known result for a vertical throw, which we have now obtained from the energy.
  4. The bar falls back to \(y = 0\) after \(2 \dot y_0/g = 1{,}0194\) s. In this time the centre of mass moves horizontally by \(2 \cdot 1{,}0194 = 2{,}0387\) m and the bar rotates by \(3 \cdot 1{,}0194 = 3{,}0581\) rad. Figure 8.34 shows the centre of mass at equal time intervals: the horizontal distances are equal because \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\) is constant, the angle grows uniformly because \(p_\varphi\) is constant, and the height follows a parabola because \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) is not constant.

The energy law and cyclic coordinates answer our question: in systems with time-independent constraints and conservative forces \(T + V\) is conserved, and for every coordinate that \(\mathcal{L}\) does not contain, one more generalized momentum is conserved. We will use the first law in section 8.12 to prove that a motion near a stable equilibrium position stays near it.

8.12 Stability of motion: Dirichlet's criterion (Dirichletov kriterij)

In section 8.6 we called an equilibrium stable when the potential energy \(V\) has a strict local minimum there (definition 8.64). That is a test for a position in which the system rests. The question we put off there is about motion: if we disturb the system slightly, for example move a pendulum a little aside or give it a small speed, does it stay near the equilibrium for all time or does it move away? We have the equations of motion since section 8.9 and conservation of energy since section 8.11, so we can now put the question precisely and answer it.

An equilibrium is a motion that does not change. Let the system have \(n\) generalized coordinates (posplošene koordinate) \(\vek q = (q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{n}})\) on an open set \(U \subset \mathbb R^n\), scleronomic ideal holonomic constraints and kinetic energy \(T = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T \mat M(\vek q)\,\dot{\vek q}\) with mass matrix \(\mat M(\vek q)\) (theorem 8.86). The matrix \(\mat M\) is symmetric and positive definite, and it is continuous because its entries are sums of products of first derivatives of the map \(\vek X\) from the definition of generalized coordinates. A motion on an interval \([0, \tau]\) is a twice continuously differentiable function \(\vek q : [0, \tau] \to U\) that satisfies Lagrange's equations (theorem 8.88). The constant function \(\vek q(t) = \vek q_0\) is a motion exactly when the generalized forces at \(\vek q_0\) are zero, since at \(\dot{\vek q} = \vek 0\) also \(\partial T/\partial\vek q = \vek 0\). For conservative forces this is the condition \(\nabla V(\vek q_0) = \vek 0\) (corollary 8.58), and uniqueness of the motion (corollary 8.94, under its smoothness assumptions) says that this is the only motion that starts at \(\vek q_0\) at rest. Such a \(\vek q_0\) we call an equilibrium.

A disturbed start is described by two numbers, the displacement \(\vek q(0) - \vek q_0\) and the initial velocity \(\dot{\vek q}(0)\). If the start is near the equilibrium in both, the motion must also stay near in both: in position and in velocity, and this on every interval on which the motion exists, with the same \(\delta\) whatever the length of the interval. For a pendulum we ask whether the angle does not grow beyond some limit and whether the pendulum does not spin too fast. Hence the definition. Coordinates may have different units (for a rod on two springs one coordinate is a displacement in metres, the other an angle in radians), so \(|\vek q|\) is the Euclidean norm of the numbers we get in the chosen units. A different choice of units changes distances only by constant factors and does not change whether stability holds.

Definition 8.114 Stable and unstable equilibrium of motion (stabilno in nestabilno ravnovesje gibanja)

Let \(\vek q_0 \in U\) be an equilibrium of a system with \(n\) generalized coordinates \(\vek q\) on an open set \(U \subset \mathbb R^n\), as described above. The equilibrium \(\vek q_0\) is stable (stabilno), if for every number \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is a number \(\delta > 0\) such that for every number \(\tau > 0\) and every motion on \([0, \tau]\) with \(|\vek q(0) - \vek q_0| < \delta\) and \(|\dot{\vek q}(0)| < \delta\)

\[|\vek q(t) - \vek q_0| < \varepsilon \quad \text{and} \quad |\dot{\vek q}(t)| < \varepsilon\]

holds for every \(t \in [0, \tau]\). The equilibrium is unstable (nestabilno) if it is not stable: there is a number \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that for every number \(\delta > 0\) there is a motion on some \([0, \tau]\) with \(|\vek q(0) - \vek q_0| < \delta\) and \(|\dot{\vek q}(0)| < \delta\) that at some moment \(t \in [0, \tau]\) has \(|\vek q(t) - \vek q_0| \ge \varepsilon\) or \(|\dot{\vek q}(t)| \ge \varepsilon\).

Source: The definition is not from a source. GR §2.1.1 (PDF p. 78) defines stability by an energy bound (remark after theorem 8.115), CK §3.3 (PDF pp. 84-86) classifies only linear systems by the roots of the characteristic equation.

The definition speaks of motions on an interval \([0, \tau]\) with arbitrary \(\tau\), because corollary 8.94 gives a motion only on some, possibly very short, interval around the initial time. In this way stability does not depend on how long the motion exists, and theorem 8.115 proves it without a theorem the book does not have. Stability is therefore a statement about all motions that exist, and does not say that they exist for all times. That would be shown by the continuation theorem for solutions, which the book does not prove (section 8.9.1, after corollary 8.94). We need it for instability (remark after theorem 8.117), not for stability.

Where the border between stable and unstable lies we see on pendulum A (a point mass \(m = 1\) kg on a rigid rod of length \(l = 1\) m). At \(\theta = 0\) the potential energy \(V = -m g l \cos\theta\) has a minimum with \(V'' = 9{,}81\) J. If we give the pendulum a slight push there, it oscillates about that position. At \(\theta = \pi\) we have \(V'' = -9{,}81\) J, and if we balance the pendulum there, an infinitely small push topples it. Dirichlet's criterion says that in the first case no motion needs to be computed, since a look at the shape of \(V\) suffices.

The idea of the proof is conservation of energy (theorem 8.106). The total energy \(\mathcal E = T + V\) stays during the motion equal to the initial one, and \(T\) cannot be negative. Hence at every moment \(V \le \mathcal E\). If the initial energy is smaller than the lowest value of \(V\) on a ball around the equilibrium, the motion cannot reach that sphere, because the potential energy there would already be more than the total energy (figure 8.35). The velocity is bounded because \(T\) is bounded by the same energy and the mass matrix is positive definite. The name Dirichlet's criterion is from the course syllabus. It is in none of the books the chapter uses, so we write nothing about its history.

Theorem 8.115 Dirichlet's stability criterion (Dirichletov kriterij stabilnosti)

Let a system with \(n\) generalized coordinates \(\vek q\) on an open set \(U \subset \mathbb R^n\) be as in definition 8.114: ideal holonomic scleronomic constraints, mass matrix \(\mat M(\vek q)\) symmetric, continuous and positive definite. Let the active forces be conservative with potential \(V(\vek q)\), continuously differentiable on \(U\), and possibly also non-conservative forces \(\vek Q^{\mathrm{nc}}\) that are dissipative, \(\vek Q^{\mathrm{nc}} \cdot \dot{\vek q} \le 0\) (section 8.11). If \(V\) has a strict local minimum at the equilibrium \(\vek q_0\) (definition 8.64), then \(\vek q_0\) is a stable equilibrium.

Proof

We must show that for every \(\varepsilon\) there is a \(\delta\) from definition 8.114. We choose it so that the initial energy is smaller than the lowest value of \(V\) on a sphere smaller than \(\varepsilon\), and than the energy at which the velocity would reach \(\varepsilon\).

  1. Instead of \(\vek q\) we write \(\vek p = \vek q - \vek q_0\) and instead of \(V\) the function \(V(\vek q_0 + \vek p) - V(\vek q_0)\), which has value 0 at \(\vek p = \vek 0\) (the potential is determined up to a constant). The energy changes by a constant, and the displacement \(|\vek p| = |\vek q - \vek q_0|\) and the velocity stay. From now on the equilibrium is at \(\vek p = \vek 0\), \(V(\vek 0) = 0\), and we write \(\mat M\) as a function of \(\vek p\).
  2. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given. Since \(V\) has a strict local minimum at \(\vek 0\), there is \(r > 0\) such that the closed ball \(|\vek p| \le r\) lies in \(U\) and \(V(\vek p) > 0\) for \(0 < |\vek p| \le r\). Let \(\rho = \min(\varepsilon, r)\). On the closed ball \(B = \{|\vek p| \le \rho\}\) we therefore have \(V \ge 0\).
  3. The sphere \(S = \{|\vek p| = \rho\}\) is nonempty, bounded and closed (lemma 8.24, item 4, since \(|\vek p|^2\) is a polynomial), \(V\) is continuous (theorem 8.27, item 2), so by theorem 8.26 \(V\) attains its smallest value \(\mu\) on \(S\). It attains it at a point with \(|\vek p| = \rho > 0\), so \(\mu > 0\).
  4. The function \((\vek p, \vek u) \mapsto \vek u^\T \mat M(\vek p)\,\vek u\) is continuous (lemmas 8.25 and 8.24, item 3) on the nonempty, closed (lemma 8.24, item 4) and bounded set \(B \times \{|\vek u| = 1\} \subset \mathbb R^{2n}\) and positive there, because \(\mat M\) is positive definite. By theorem 8.26 it has a smallest value \(m_0 > 0\) and a largest \(m_1\). For \(|\vek p| \le \rho\) and every \(\dot{\vek p}\) we therefore have \(\tfrac12 m_0 |\dot{\vek p}|^2 \le T \le \tfrac12 m_1 |\dot{\vek p}|^2\).
  5. Let \(\bar\mu = \min\bigl(\mu,\ \tfrac12 m_0 \varepsilon^2\bigr)\). Since \(V\) is continuous at \(\vek 0\) with value 0, there is \(\delta_1 \in (0, \rho]\) such that \(V(\vek p) < \bar\mu/2\) for \(|\vek p| < \delta_1\). Let \(\delta_2 = \sqrt{\bar\mu/m_1}\) and \(\delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2)\). For a start with \(|\vek p(0)| < \delta\) and \(|\dot{\vek p}(0)| < \delta\) we have by step 4 \(T(0) \le \tfrac12 m_1 \delta^2 < \bar\mu/2\) and \(V(\vek p(0)) < \bar\mu/2\), so \(\mathcal E(0) < \bar\mu \le \mu\).
  6. A motion on \([0, \tau]\) satisfies theorem 8.106: the total energy \(\mathcal E = T + V\) does not increase for dissipative forces and is constant for conservative ones only. Hence \(\mathcal E(t) \le \mathcal E(0)\) for every \(t \in [0, \tau]\).
  7. We show \(|\vek p(t)| < \rho\) for every \(t \in [0, \tau]\). Suppose that for some \(t_1 \in [0, \tau]\) this is not so. The function \(g(t) = |\vek p(t)|\) is continuous, \(g(0) < \delta \le \rho\) and \(g(t_1) \ge \rho\), so by theorem 2.57 there is \(s \in (0, t_1]\) with \(g(s) = \rho\), so \(\vek p(s) \in S\) and \(V(\vek p(s)) \ge \mu\) by step 3. Since \(T \ge 0\) and by step 6, \(V(\vek p(s)) = \mathcal E(s) - T(s) \le \mathcal E(0) < \mu\). This is a contradiction.
  8. Hence \(|\vek q(t) - \vek q_0| = |\vek p(t)| < \rho \le \varepsilon\) for every \(t \in [0, \tau]\). In the ball \(V \ge 0\), so by step 6 \(T(t) = \mathcal E(t) - V(\vek p(t)) \le \mathcal E(0) < \bar\mu \le \tfrac12 m_0 \varepsilon^2\). By step 4, \(\tfrac12 m_0 |\dot{\vek q}|^2 \le T < \tfrac12 m_0 \varepsilon^2\), so \(|\dot{\vek q}(t)| < \varepsilon\).

Source: The proof is not from a source, no such criterion under the name Dirichlet is in the sources of the project (index.md, gap). GR §2.1.1 (PDF p. 78) uses the same idea, conservation of energy \(\mathcal E = T + V\) (2.4) and \(V \ge 0\) (2.5) around the equilibrium.

The proof showed that the motion cannot escape, because to do so it would have to climb the rim of the potential valley, for which it lacks the energy. Step 3 is essential: we need a strict minimum, since at \(\mu = 0\) (for example if \(V\) were 0 along a line through \(\vek q_0\)) the initial energy could not be smaller than \(\mu\). Step 7 uses the intermediate value theorem on the continuous function \(|\vek p(t)|\), so the motion cannot "jump over" the sphere. The requirement \(\vek Q^{\mathrm{nc}} \cdot \dot{\vek q} \le 0\) is met by forces that brake (viscous friction, air resistance): their power only decreases the energy (theorem 8.106). In this case the motion stays near, but does not necessarily return to the equilibrium. How it really settles into the equilibrium is the subject of chapter 9.

GR (PDF p. 78) defines stability as follows: the equilibrium is stable when there is an energy bound \(\mathcal E^*\) such that for every initial energy \(\mathcal E < \mathcal E^*\) at all later moments \(V \le \mathcal E\) holds, with equality only at the equilibrium. That inequality is from step 7 (the energy stays, \(T \ge 0\)). Our definition requires more: that also the displacement and the velocity stay small, and this is proved by steps 3, 7 and 8.

Example 8.116 Stable equilibria on three examples (stabilna ravnovesja na treh primerih)

Let us take three systems from section 8.6 and in each find \(\delta\) for the chosen \(\varepsilon\) following the steps of the proof.

  1. Pendulum A at \(\theta = 0\). With \(m = 1\) kg, \(l = 1\) m we have \(V(\theta) = 9{,}81\,(1 - \cos\theta)\) J (potential shifted to 0) and \(m_0 = m_1 = m\,l^2 = 1\) kg m². We choose \(\varepsilon = 0{,}1\) rad. \(V > 0\) for \(0 < |\theta| < 2\pi\), so \(\rho = \varepsilon\). The smallest value on \(S = \{\pm 0{,}1\}\) is \(\mu = V(0{,}1) = 0{,}04901\) J, and \(\tfrac12 m_0 \varepsilon^2 = 0{,}005\) J is smaller, so \(\bar\mu = 0{,}005\) J. From \(V(\theta) < \bar\mu/2 = 0{,}0025\) J it follows that \(\delta_1 = 0{,}02258\) rad, and from \(\delta_2 = \sqrt{\bar\mu/m_1} = 0{,}0707\) 1/s we see that \(\delta = \delta_1\). A pendulum released with a displacement smaller than \(0{,}0226\) rad (\(1{,}29^\circ\)) and a velocity smaller than \(0{,}0226\) 1/s therefore never exceeds a displacement of \(0{,}1\) rad (\(5{,}7^\circ\)) and a velocity of \(0{,}1\) 1/s. The estimate is very cautious. A computation of motions from five starts on the edge of the set \(\delta\) (\(\vek p(0) = (\delta, 0)\), \((0, \delta)\) and three others) gives the largest displacement \(0{,}0235\) rad and the largest velocity \(0{,}0735\) 1/s.
  2. Inverted rod B at \(P = 1000\) N. With \(k_{\mathrm{r}} = 2000\) N m, \(L = 1\) m and a point mass \(m = 10\) kg at the top we have \(V(\theta) = \tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{r}}\theta^2 + P L(\cos\theta - 1)\) and \(V''(0) = k_{\mathrm{r}} - P L = 1000\) N m > 0, which by section 8.6 is a strict minimum. The mass is \(m L^2 = 10\) kg m². At \(\varepsilon = 0{,}1\) rad we have \(\mu = V(0{,}1) = 5{,}004\) J, \(\tfrac12 m_0\varepsilon^2 = 0{,}05\) J, so \(\bar\mu = 0{,}05\) J. From \(V < 0{,}025\) J it follows that \(\delta_1 = 0{,}00707\) rad (as for the parabola \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1000\,\theta^2\)), \(\delta_2 = \sqrt{0{,}05/10} = 0{,}0707\) 1/s, so \(\delta = 0{,}00707\). At \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 2000\) N we have \(V''(0) = 0\) and the second derivative says nothing (section 8.6), but \(V(\theta) = 1000\,\theta^2 + 2000\,(\cos\theta - 1) \approx 83{,}3\,\theta^4\) has a strict minimum. Theorem 8.115 is satisfied by this: \(\mu = V(0{,}1) = 0{,}00833\) J is smaller than \(0{,}05\) J, \(\bar\mu = 0{,}00833\) J, \(\delta_1 = 0{,}0841\) rad, \(\delta_2 = 0{,}0289\) 1/s. The theorem also covers the case that the second derivative could not decide.
  3. Toggle mechanism D at \(P = 100\) N, equilibrium \(\theta = 0{,}50523\) rad (\(28{,}95^\circ\)). Here \(V'' = 2239{,}3\) J (section 8.6) and \(m(\theta) = \tfrac13 + 2\sin^2\theta\) kg m². At \(\varepsilon = 0{,}05\) rad on the interval \([\theta_0 - \varepsilon, \theta_0 + \varepsilon]\) we always have \(V'' \ge 1622\) J, so \(V > V(\theta_0)\) everywhere except at \(\theta_0\) (Taylor's theorem 8.60 with remainder). The mass lies between \(m_0 = 0{,}7199\) and \(m_1 = 0{,}8891\) kg m². The smaller of the values of \(V - V(\theta_0)\) at the two ends of the interval is \(\mu = 2{,}538\) J, and \(\tfrac12 m_0\varepsilon^2 = 0{,}0009\) J is smaller, so \(\bar\mu = 0{,}0009\) J. We get \(\delta_1 = 0{,}000634\) rad and \(\delta_2 = 0{,}0318\) 1/s, so \(\delta = 0{,}000634\) rad (\(0{,}036^\circ\)). The same computation holds at the equilibrium \(-30{,}94^\circ\) with \(V'' = 2741\) J. The computed motions from starts on the border \(\delta\) stay below \(0{,}00064\) rad and \(0{,}034\) 1/s, the velocity also below the bound \(\varepsilon = 0{,}05\) 1/s.

In the third example \(\delta\) is small because in the same circle we mix a displacement in radians and a velocity in 1/s. The kinetic energy \(\tfrac12 m_0\varepsilon^2 = 0{,}0009\) J is there much smaller than \(\mu = 2{,}5\) J, so the kinetic energy limits \(\bar\mu\) and with it \(\delta\). This is the price of a simple estimate, it does not affect the stability of the equilibrium.

The criterion says when an equilibrium is stable. But what if it is not a minimum? For pendulum A at \(\theta = \pi\) we have \(V'' < 0\). Let the pendulum start at \(\theta = \pi\) with a small velocity \(v_0\) and let us compute when it moves away by \(\varepsilon = 0{,}1\) rad (numerical integration of the equation of motion):

\(v_0\) (1/s) time to displacement \(0{,}1\) rad (s)
\(10^{-2}\) \(1{,}32\)
\(10^{-4}\) \(2{,}79\)
\(10^{-6}\) \(4{,}26\)

Each time we reduce the initial velocity by a factor of 100, the time grows by the same increment, \(1{,}47\) s. For uniform motion with the initial velocity the times would be \(0{,}1/v_0\), that is 10 s, 1000 s and 100 000 s. The reason for the slower growth is the force that pulls the pendulum away from the top: at displacement \(p\) its component is \(m g \sin p \approx m g\,p\), so the larger the distance, the larger the acceleration away. The velocity therefore grows faster and faster, and even a very small initial push does not hold back the departure for long. The function that describes this growth exactly is met in this book only with damping (chapter 9). Here we show only that the displacement leaves the circle in a finite time, and estimate the time from above.

Theorem 8.117 Instability for one degree of freedom (nestabilnost pri eni prostostni stopnji)

Let a system have one generalized coordinate \(q\) on an open interval \(U\), scleronomic ideal holonomic constraints, kinetic energy \(T = \tfrac12 m(q)\,\dot q^2\) with continuous function \(m > 0\) and only conservative active forces with potential \(V\), twice continuously differentiable on \(U\). Let \(q_0 \in U\) be an equilibrium, \(V'(q_0) = 0\), and \(V''(q_0) < 0\). Then there is \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that for every number \(v_0 > 0\) every motion on \([0, \varepsilon/c]\) with \(q(0) = q_0\) and \(\dot q(0) = v_0\) reaches the displacement \(\varepsilon\), that is \(q(t) = q_0 + \varepsilon\) at some \(t \le \varepsilon/c\), where \(c = v_0\sqrt{m(q_0)/m_1}\) and \(m_1\) is the largest value of the function \(m\) on \([q_0 - \varepsilon, q_0 + \varepsilon]\). The equilibrium \(q_0\) is therefore unstable if for every such \(v_0\) such a motion exists.

Proof

We must show that a motion that starts at \(q_0\) with an arbitrarily small velocity leaves an interval around \(q_0\). Energy shows that the motion cannot stop, since near \(q_0\) always \(V < V(q_0)\).

  1. Since \(V''\) is continuous and \(V''(q_0) < 0\), there is \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that the closed interval \(I = [q_0 - \varepsilon, q_0 + \varepsilon]\) lies in \(U\) and \(V'' < 0\) on \(I\). By Taylor's theorem (theorem 8.60) with \(V'(q_0) = 0\) we have \(V(q) = V(q_0) + \tfrac12 V''(c)(q - q_0)^2\) for some \(c\) between \(q_0\) and \(q\), so \(V(q) < V(q_0)\) for \(q \in I\), \(q \ne q_0\).
  2. Let \(m_1\) be the largest value of the function \(m\) on \(I\) (theorem 1.73, the extreme value theorem).
  3. Let \(q(0) = q_0\), \(\dot q(0) = v_0 > 0\). By theorem 8.106 \(\tfrac12 m(q)\,\dot q^2 + V(q) = V(q_0) + \tfrac12 m(q_0) v_0^2\) at every moment. As long as \(q(t) \in I\), we therefore have \(\tfrac12 m(q)\,\dot q^2 = \tfrac12 m(q_0)\,v_0^2 + \bigl(V(q_0) - V(q)\bigr) \ge \tfrac12 m(q_0)\,v_0^2 > 0\), so \(\dot q \ne 0\).
  4. Let \(q(t) \in I\) for every \(t \in [0, t']\). The function \(\dot q\) is continuous and \(\dot q(0) = v_0 > 0\). If it were negative at some moment of \([0, t']\), by theorem 2.57 it would have a zero, which step 3 excludes. Hence \(\dot q > 0\) on \([0, t']\) and by step 3 also \(\dot q^2 \ge m(q_0)\,v_0^2/m(q) \ge m(q_0)\,v_0^2/m_1 = c^2\), so \(\dot q \ge c\) as long as \(q \in I\).
  5. Let \(t^*\) be the largest time in \([0, \varepsilon/c]\) up to which \(q\) stays in \(I\) (the set of such times is closed, because \(q\) is continuous and \(I\) is closed, and it contains 0). By the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) \(q(t^*) - q_0 \ge c\,t^*\). If \(t^* < \varepsilon/c\), \(q(t^*)\) is not an interior point of the interval \(I\) (otherwise \(q\) would stay in \(I\) a little longer), and since \(q(t^*) > q_0\), we have \(q(t^*) = q_0 + \varepsilon\). If \(t^* = \varepsilon/c\), then \(q(t^*) - q_0 \ge \varepsilon\) and \(q(t^*) \in I\), so again \(q(t^*) = q_0 + \varepsilon\). In both cases the motion reaches the displacement \(\varepsilon\) at time \(t^* \le \varepsilon/c\), which is the claim. Since \(v_0\) is arbitrarily small, this means instability, if the motion on \([0, \varepsilon/c]\) exists.

Source: The proof is not from a source (index.md, gap). GR §2.1.1 (PDF p. 78) states that a stable equilibrium corresponds to a local minimum of \(V\), but does not prove instability.

The proof showed that at \(V'' < 0\) the energy itself drives the motion away from the equilibrium: where \(V\) is lower than at \(q_0\), \(T\) must be larger than the initial one, and the velocity cannot change sign. The estimate \(\varepsilon/c\) is an upper bound of the time, since it computes as if the velocity did not increase. The theorem proves that every motion that exists up to time \(\varepsilon/c\) reaches the displacement.
