For the swing from \(90^\circ\) the estimate with \(\cos\theta \le 1\) does not decide, but the computation from section 8.10 gave for the parabola \(\eta\) the second variation \(2 \cdot (-0{,}9945) = -1{,}989\) J s (NumPy), so negative. The action is stationary in both windows, but the second variation is positive for every variation only in the shorter one. The same inequality will decide on buckling.

8.14.2 Cantilever column (konzolni steber)

We start with the column that is clamped at \(s = 0\) and has a free top, loaded with a vertical force \(P\) (figure 8.41). The column is inextensible, so the angle during buckling is most easily described by the angle of the tangent to the axis and not by the displacement. Let \(s\) be the arc length of the axis from the clamp, \(0 \le s \le L\), and \(\theta(s)\) the angle between the tangent of the axis and the vertical. The tangent has the component \(\cos\theta\) vertically and \(\sin\theta\) horizontally. At the clamp the tangent is vertical, \(\theta(0) = 0\). We introduced the curvature of the axis in definition 5.16 as \(v''\) for small slopes and explained it as the change of slope per unit length. For large slopes we take as the curvature the change of the angle of the tangent per unit of arc length, \(\theta'(s)\). This is the exact curvature of the axis, which SADD (PDF p. 578) writes as \(v''/(1 + v'^2)^{3/2}\). For small slopes it agrees with \(v''\), because then the angle of the tangent is almost equal to the slope and the arc length almost equal to the length along the straight line, at \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) with a difference of at most 1,5 % as in chapter 5.

We write the energy without approximation. The bending energy of the axis is \(\int_0^L \tfrac12 EI\,\theta'^2\,\mathrm{d}s\) (the energy of a beam from section 5.12.1 with the curvature \(\theta'\)). Here we assume that the moment is proportional to the curvature, \(M = EI\,\theta'\), also at a large slope, as Euler did (historical box in section 5.9). The axis is parametrized by arc length \(s\), so it has the unit tangent \((\sin\theta, \cos\theta)\) and the vertical coordinate of the point has the derivative \(\cos\theta(s)\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40) the height of the point at arc length \(s\) is \(\int_0^s\cos\theta(\sigma)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\), so the top drops by \(\Delta = \int_0^L (1 - \cos\theta)\,\mathrm{d}s\). The vertical force \(P\), which points downward, has the potential energy \(P\) times the height of the point of application, like a weight, so the energy of the force decreases by \(P\,\Delta\). The total potential energy is

\[\Pi(\theta) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EI\,\theta'^2\,\mathrm{d}s - P \int_0^L (1 - \cos\theta)\,\mathrm{d}s , \qquad \theta(0) = 0 . \tag{8.117}\]

Admissible functions are \(\theta\) with continuous first two derivatives and \(\theta(0) = 0\). The straight position \(\theta = 0\) has \(\Pi = 0\). Is it an equilibrium and when is it stable?

Theorem 8.130 Equilibrium of the cantilever column (ravnovesje konzolnega stebra)

An admissible function \(\theta\) is a stationary point of the functional (8.117) exactly when it satisfies

\[EI\,\theta'' + P\sin\theta = 0 \quad \text{on } [0, L] , \qquad \theta'(L) = 0 . \tag{8.118}\]
Proof

We must show that this follows from theorem 5.69.

  1. The functional (8.117) is of the form (5.63) with the independent variable \(s\) instead of \(x\), the function \(\theta\) instead of \(v\) and \(F(s, \theta, p) = \tfrac12 EI\,p^2 - P(1 - \cos\theta)\), without a term with the second derivative and without loads at the ends. The partial derivatives are \(F_\theta = -P\sin\theta\) and \(F_{\mathrm{p}} = EI\,p\), \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\).
  2. The equation (5.64) is \(\hat F_\theta - \hat F_{\mathrm{p}}{}' = 0\), that is \(-P\sin\theta - EI\,\theta'' = 0\).
  3. The value \(\theta(L)\) is not prescribed, so at \(s = L\) the natural condition is \(\hat F_{\mathrm{p}} - \hat F_{\mathrm{r}}{}' = f_{\mathrm{L}}\) with \(f_{\mathrm{L}} = 0\), that is \(EI\,\theta'(L) = 0\). The values \(\theta'(0)\) and \(\theta'(L)\) are not prescribed, and their natural conditions \(\hat F_{\mathrm{r}} = -\mu_0\) and \(\hat F_{\mathrm{r}} = \mu_{\mathrm{L}}\) are satisfied by themselves, because \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) and \(\mu_0 = \mu_{\mathrm{L}} = 0\). The essential condition \(\theta(0) = 0\) is in the set of admissible functions.

Source: The proof is not from a source, it uses theorem 5.69 from chapter 5. The equation with the exact curvature was integrated by Lagrange with a series (TIMO, PDF p. 47).

The natural condition \(\theta'(L) = 0\) says that the curvature, and so the moment \(EI\,\theta'\), is zero at the free top, as it must be. The straight position \(\theta = 0\) satisfies the equation at every force \(P\). The equation \(EI\,\theta'' + P\sin\theta = 0\) is the pendulum equation from example A, \(\ddot\theta + (g/l)\sin\theta = 0\), with the arc length \(s\) instead of time and \(P/EI\) instead of \(g/l\). For small angles we replace \(\sin\theta\) by \(\theta\), and the discarded part is by lemma 8.19 at most \(|\theta|^3/6\). We get the linearized equation \(\theta'' + k^2\theta = 0\) with \(k^2 = P/EI\). Its solutions are \(A\cos ks + B\sin ks\) (theorem 8.17), the condition \(\theta(0) = 0\) gives \(A = 0\) and the condition at the top gives \(B\,k\cos kL = 0\). A nonzero solution exists if \(\cos kL = 0\), so \(kL = \pi/2\), \(3\pi/2\), \(\dots\) The smallest force at which the linearized equation has a curved solution is

\[P_{\mathrm{cr}} = EI\,\Big(\frac{\pi}{2L}\Big)^2 = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{4L^2} . \tag{8.119}\]

For the strip from section 5.1.3, bent about the weak axis, with \(L = 1\) m, \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 12\,896\) N (NumPy). The stress in the column is then \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}/A = 16{,}1\) MPa, so 7 % of the yield limit. Up to the critical force the material stays far below the yield limit: it is bent by shape, not by strength.

This is Euler's view: we look for the force at which the straight position has another, curved equilibrium position nearby. Is this force also the limit of stability? Energy answers, as in section 8.6. Definition 8.64 is stated for finitely many coordinates, so for a column we ask something stronger: whether the energy at every other admissible shape is larger than the energy of the straight position.

Theorem 8.131 Stability of the cantilever column (stabilnost konzolnega stebra)

Let \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/(4L^2)\).

(a) If \(P < P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), then \(\Pi(\theta) > 0 = \Pi(0)\) for every admissible function \(\theta \ne 0\).

(b) If \(P > P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), then for every number \(\varepsilon \in (0, \sqrt{6(P - P_{\mathrm{cr}})/P})\) there is an admissible function \(\theta\) with \(\max|\theta| = \varepsilon\) and \(\Pi(\theta) < 0\).

(c) If \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), then \(\Pi(\theta) > 0\) for every admissible function \(\theta \ne 0\).

Proof

We must show a lower estimate of the energy in cases (a) and (c) and a function with negative energy in case (b). In both we use the bounds for the cosine from lemma 8.19.

  1. By lemma 8.19, \(1 - \cos t \le t^2/2\) for every \(t\). If in this lemma we integrate \(\sin t \ge t - t^3/6\), we get \(1 - \cos t \ge t^2/2 - t^4/24\) for \(t \ge 0\), and by evenness of the cosine for every \(t\).
  2. (a) From \(1 - \cos\theta \le \theta^2/2\), \(\Pi(\theta) \ge \tfrac12\int_0^L (EI\,\theta'^2 - P\,\theta^2)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  3. Lemma 8.127 in case (b) with \(\ell = L\) and \(k = \pi/(2L)\) gives \(\int\theta^2 \le (2L/\pi)^2\int\theta'^2\). Therefore \(\Pi(\theta) \ge \tfrac12\,\big(EI - P\,(2L/\pi)^2\big)\int\theta'^2 = \tfrac12\,EI\,(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\int\theta'^2\).
  4. If \(\int\theta'^2 = 0\), then \(\theta' = 0\) (a continuous nonnegative function), so \(\theta\) is constant and by \(\theta(0) = 0\) zero. For \(\theta \ne 0\) therefore \(\int\theta'^2 > 0\) and \(\Pi(\theta) > 0\).
  5. (b) Let \(\eta(s) = \sin\big(\pi s/(2L)\big)\) and \(\theta = \varepsilon\eta\). This is admissible, \(\max|\theta| = \varepsilon\). By step 9 of the proof of lemma 8.127 with \(c = 1\) and \(\ell = L\), \(\int\eta'^2 = k^2 L/2\) and \(\int\eta^2 = L/2\) with \(k = \pi/(2L)\), so \(\int(EI\,\eta'^2 - P\,\eta^2) = (EI\,k^2 - P)\,L/2 = -(P - P_{\mathrm{cr}})\,L/2\).
  6. By step 1, \(\Pi(\varepsilon\eta) \le \tfrac12\varepsilon^2\int(EI\,\eta'^2 - P\,\eta^2) + \tfrac{P}{24}\,\varepsilon^4\int\eta^4\). Since \(\eta^4 \le 1\), \(\int\eta^4 \le L\) and \(\Pi(\varepsilon\eta) \le -\tfrac14\,\varepsilon^2 (P - P_{\mathrm{cr}})\,L + \tfrac{P}{24}\,\varepsilon^4 L = \tfrac14\,\varepsilon^2 L\,\big(-(P - P_{\mathrm{cr}}) + P\,\varepsilon^2/6\big)\).
  7. The bracket is negative for \(\varepsilon^2 < 6(P - P_{\mathrm{cr}})/P\), so \(\Pi(\varepsilon\eta) < 0\).
  8. (c) Let \(g(t) = t^2/2 - (1 - \cos t)\). We have \(g(0) = 0\) and \(g'(t) = t - \sin t > 0\) for \(t > 0\): for \(0 < t \le \pi\) as in example 8.66, and for \(t > \pi\) we have \(\sin t \le 1 < t\). By the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84), \(g(t) > 0\) for \(t > 0\), and since \(g\) is even, for every \(t \ne 0\).
  9. At \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), \(\Pi(\theta) = \tfrac12\int_0^L (EI\,\theta'^2 - P_{\mathrm{cr}}\,\theta^2)\,\mathrm{d}s + P_{\mathrm{cr}}\int_0^L g(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}s\). The first integral is not negative by step 3 with \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). The function \(g(\theta(s))\) is continuous, nonnegative and positive at a point where \(\theta(s) \ne 0\), so it has a positive integral (lemma 3.39, point 4). Hence \(\Pi(\theta) > 0\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The energy demand for a minimum is the criterion from EP (p. 180) and GR (PDF p. 78), as in section 8.6.

The theorem showed that the critical load (kritična sila) \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) from the direct search for a curved equilibrium position is at the same time the limit of energy stability. Below the limit the straight position is the lowest point of the energy, not only nearby but among all admissible shapes. Above the limit there is an arbitrarily small displacement with smaller energy. For \(P = 1{,}1\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) this is every displacement below \(\varepsilon = 0{,}74\) rad. And at \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\)? The second variation \(\int (EI\,\eta'^2 - P_{\mathrm{cr}}\,\eta^2)\) is there not negative, and for the sine \(\eta = \sin(\pi s/(2L))\) it is zero (equality in lemma 8.127), so it does not decide by itself. The exact energy decides: by point (c) the straight position is still the lowest point of the energy. The energy, however, no longer grows with the square of the displacement in the direction of the sine, only with the fourth power, since by step 6 \(\Pi(\varepsilon\eta) \le \tfrac{P_{\mathrm{cr}}}{24}\,\varepsilon^4 L\). The same holds in example B, where at \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) the second derivative is \(V''(0) = 0\), and the difference \(V(\theta) - V(0) = P_{\mathrm{cr}}L\,g(\theta)\) is positive by step 8. What the theorem does not say: whether a column that we disturb moves near the straight position. Dirichlet's criterion (theorem 8.115) we proved for finitely many coordinates, for a continuous column we do not claim it here, and the motion of the column is treated by chapter 13. In example B, however, we already know that the frequency falls toward zero as the force approaches the limit (section 8.13).

Example B is a column with a single spring. How close does it come to a real column if we add links? Let the column be divided into \(n\) equal rigid links of length \(h = L/n\) with torsional springs at the clamp and at each of the \(n - 1\) inner joints. The model is ours. The spring has stiffness \(EI/h\), because a piece of axis of length \(h\) with constant curvature \(\Delta\theta/h\) stores the energy \(\tfrac12 EI\,(\Delta\theta/h)^2\,h = \tfrac12\,(EI/h)\,\Delta\theta^2\). Let \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) be the angle of the \(i\)-th link to the vertical and \(\theta_0 = 0\). The energy is

\[\Pi = \frac{EI}{2h}\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n}(\theta_{\mathrm{i}} - \theta_{\mathrm{i}-1})^2 - P\,h\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{n}(1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{i}}) ,\]

since link \(i\) is shorter in the vertical direction by \(h\,(1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{i}})\) and the top drops by the sum of these shortenings. For small angles \(1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{i}} \approx \theta_{\mathrm{i}}^2/2\) (lemma 8.19, the error is a quartic term). The straight position is at the limit when the quadratic form has a nonzero null vector, that is when \(P\,h^2/EI\) equals the smallest value of the quotient \(\sum(\theta_{\mathrm{i}} - \theta_{\mathrm{i}-1})^2\big/\sum\theta_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), or \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}L^2/EI = n^2\min\). For \(n = 1\) the quotient is \(1\) and this is example B with \(k_{\mathrm{r}} = EI/L\), \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}L^2/EI = 1\). For \(n = 2\) the quadratic form is \(2\theta_1^2 - 2\theta_1\theta_2 + \theta_2^2\) with the matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\), whose eigenvalues are \((3 \pm \sqrt5)/2\), the smallest \(0{,}382\), so \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}L^2/EI = 4\cdot 0{,}382 = 1{,}528\). For larger \(n\) the computation with NumPy gives:

\(n\) 1 2 3 4 8 16 \(\to\infty\)
\(P_{\mathrm{cr}}L^2/EI\) 1 1,528 1,783 1,930 2,179 2,318 \(\pi^2/4 = 2{,}467\)
share of \(\pi^2/4\) 0,405 0,619 0,722 0,782 0,883 0,940 1

The sequence grows toward \(\pi^2/4\) (figure 8.42). Why is every chain below the true value? The chain is softer than the column: the angle may jump at a joint at the price of the spring \(EI/h\), while in a continuous column a jump would mean infinite curvature and infinite energy. As we add links, the springs stiffen (\(EI/h\) grows) and jumps become ever dearer, so the threshold approaches the column. For \(n = 1\) the threshold is \(1/(\pi^2/4) = 0{,}405\) of the true value.

What happens above the limit? The linearized equation does not say, so we solve the exact equation (8.118). It is a pendulum equation, which by section 8.13 has a period that depends on the amplitude. So we expect that the force at which the angle at the top of the column equals \(\alpha\) also differs from \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\).

Theorem 8.132 Elastica of the cantilever column (elastika konzolnega stebra)

Let \(P > 0\) and \(\theta\) a solution of equation (8.118) with \(\theta(0) = 0\) and \(\theta'(L) = 0\), which is strictly increasing on \([0, L]\) and has at the top the angle \(\theta(L) = \alpha\), \(0 < \alpha < \pi\). Let \(k = \sin(\alpha/2)\) and \(K(k)\) the complete elliptic integral of the first kind (popolni eliptični integral prve vrste),

\[K(k) = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 v}}\,\mathrm{d}v .\]

Then \(P = EI\,K(k)^2/L^2\), so

\[\frac{P}{P_{\mathrm{cr}}} = \Big(\frac{2\,K(k)}{\pi}\Big)^2 > 1 . \tag{8.120}\]
Proof

We must show that the first integral of the equation gives the derivative of the angle, and that with a change of variable the arc length becomes the integral \(K\). The steps are the same as in the proof of theorem 8.123, with arc length \(s\) instead of time, \(L\) instead of \(t_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(\alpha\) instead of \(a\) and \(P/EI\) instead of \(g/l\). The shape of the axis \(\theta(s)\) is called the elastica (elastika).

  1. We multiply the equation by \(\theta'\). By the product rule, the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 3) and theorem 8.12, \(\big(\tfrac12 EI\,\theta'^2 - P\cos\theta\big)' = \theta'\,\big(EI\,\theta'' + P\sin\theta\big) = 0\) on \([0, L]\). By corollary 1.85 the expression in the bracket is constant.
  2. At \(s = L\), \(\theta'(L) = 0\) and \(\theta(L) = \alpha\), so this constant is \(-P\cos\alpha\) and \(\tfrac12 EI\,\theta'^2 = P(\cos\theta - \cos\alpha)\) on \([0, L]\).
  3. Since \(\theta\) is strictly increasing, for \(0 \le s < L\) the angle is \(0 \le \theta(s) < \alpha < \pi\) and by lemma 8.10, point 3, \(\cos\theta(s) > \cos\alpha\). Difference quotients of an increasing function are not negative, so \(\theta' \ge 0\) and by step 2 \(\theta' = \sqrt{2P/EI}\,\sqrt{\cos\theta - \cos\alpha} > 0\) on \([0, L)\).
  4. As in step 3 of the proof of theorem 8.123, \(\cos\theta - \cos\alpha = 2\big(k^2 - \sin^2(\theta/2)\big)\), and \(0 < k < 1\), because \(0 < \alpha/2 < \pi/2\). Let \(h\) be the inverse function of the sine on \([0, \pi/2]\) as in step 4 there and \(u(s) = h\big(\sin(\theta(s)/2)/k\big)\). For \(s \in [0, L)\), \(0 \le \sin(\theta/2)/k < 1\), so \(u \in [0, \pi/2)\) and \(\sin u = \sin(\theta/2)/k\). The function \(u\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), \(u(0) = 0\) and \(u(L) = h(1) = \pi/2\). As in step 5 there, \(\cos^2(\theta/2) = 1 - k^2\sin^2 u\) and \(\cos\theta - \cos\alpha = 2k^2\cos^2 u\), so by step 3 \(\theta' = 2k\sqrt{P/EI}\,\cos u\).
  5. On \((0, L)\), \(0 < \sin(\theta/2)/k < 1\), so \(u\) is differentiable there by the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 3) and the derivative of the inverse function \(h'(y) = 1/\cos h(y)\): \(u' = \dfrac{1}{\cos u}\cdot\dfrac{\cos(\theta/2)\,\theta'}{2k} = \sqrt{P/EI}\,\cos(\theta/2) = \sqrt{P/EI}\,\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 u}\), where we inserted step 4 and used \(\cos(\theta/2) > 0\), because \(\theta/2 < \pi/2\).
  6. Let \(F(u) = \int_0^u \mathrm{d}v\big/\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 v}\). Since \(1 - k^2\sin^2 v \ge 1 - k^2 > 0\), the integrand is continuous on \([0, \pi/2]\) and \(F' = 1/\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 u}\) (theorem 3.40). The function \(G(s) = F(u(s))\) is continuous on \([0, L]\) with \(G(0) = 0\), and on \((0, L)\) it has by the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 3) and step 5 the derivative \(G' = u'\big/\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 u} = \sqrt{P/EI}\).
  7. The function \(G(s) - \sqrt{P/EI}\,s\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), has zero derivative on \((0, L)\) and is zero at \(0\), so by corollary 1.85 it is zero on \([0, L]\). At \(s = L\), \(G(L) = F(\pi/2) = K(k)\), so \(K(k) = \sqrt{P/EI}\,L\) and \(P = EI\,K^2/L^2\). Division by \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/(4L^2)\) gives (8.120).
  8. For \(0 < k < 1\) the function \(1/\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 v} - 1\) is continuous, nonnegative and positive at \(v = \pi/2\), so it has a positive integral (lemma 3.39, point 4). Hence \(K(k) > \int_0^{\pi/2} 1\,\mathrm{d}v = \pi/2\) and \(P > P_{\mathrm{cr}}\).

Source: BOWER §10.4.3 (PDF p. 677 and 678) treats an inextensible bar with pinned ends. For the shape with \(n\) half-waves it gives the relation \(L\sqrt{P/EI_2} = 2nK(k_{\mathrm{n}})\) with the complete elliptic integral of the first kind \(K\), where \(L\) is the length of the bar, and the angle \(\theta = 2\sin^{-1}\{k_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{sn}(\dots)\}\), so \(k_{\mathrm{n}}\) is like our \(k\) the sine of half the largest angle. A bar of length \(2L\) with one half-wave is composed of two of our cantilevers of length \(L\) clamped in its middle, and the relation with \(n = 1\) and length \(2L\) is our \(L\sqrt{P/EI} = K\). BOWER also states that \(K\) has the smallest value \(\pi/2\) at \(k = 0\) and grows with \(k\), and that for \(P < \pi^2 EI_2/L^2\) there are no curved equilibria. The proof by steps is ours, with the same substitution \(\sin(\theta/2) = k\sin u\) as in GR (example 1.7, PDF p. 49 and 50) and in theorem 8.123.

How fast does the force grow with the displacement? For small \(k\) the integrand \(1/\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 v}\) is approximately \(1 + \tfrac12 k^2\sin^2 v\), the integral of \(\sin^2 v\) over \([0, \pi/2]\) is \(\pi/4\) (as for the period in section 8.13), so \(K \approx \tfrac\pi2(1 + k^2/4)\) and \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}} \approx 1 + k^2/2 \approx 1 + \alpha^2/8\), since \(k \approx \alpha/2\). The neglected terms are of fourth order in \(k\). At \(\alpha = 10^\circ\), \(\alpha^2/8 = 0{,}0038\) and the exact value is likewise \(0{,}0038\), at \(30^\circ\) it is \(0{,}0343\) against the exact \(0{,}0351\) (error \(2{,}4\) %). Above the limit therefore an already very slightly larger force gives a large bending: at a force only \(0{,}38\) % above the critical one the angle at the top is already \(10^\circ\). Curved equilibria exist only above \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). Such a bifurcation (razcep), in which the curved positions appear at a force larger than the critical one, is called supercritical (nadkritični), as in example B (example 8.66).

The numbers in the figure are computed by integrating equation (8.118) with the RK4 method (20 000 steps) with the initial derivative \(\theta'(0) = \sqrt{2P(1 - \cos\alpha)/EI}\) from the second step of the proof. The ratios \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) are the squares of the ratios \(2K/\pi\) between the period of the pendulum and its value for small amplitudes in example A: \(1{,}0019^2\) at \(10^\circ\) (period increase \(0{,}19\) %), \(1{,}0174^2\) at \(30^\circ\) and \(1{,}1803^2\) at \(90^\circ\). The equations are the same.

How far may a column in fact bend? The most loaded are the outer fibres at the clamp. There the moment is \(M = P\,\delta\) with the displacement of the top \(\delta\) (the force \(P\) has the arm \(\delta\)), the outer fibre is half the thickness \(b/2 = 10\) mm from the axis. The stress is \(\sigma = P/A + P\,\delta\,(b/2)/I_{\mathrm{y}}\) (the axial and bending stress add on the compressed side, as with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A - M y/I\) from chapter 5, here about the weak axis). At \(\delta = 42{,}1\) mm this is \(16{,}1 + 203{,}8 = 219{,}9\) MPa, so the yield limit. This is a top angle of \(3{,}79^\circ\) and \(P = 1{,}0005\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). The elastic story ends already at a displacement of 42 mm, when the force is only \(0{,}05\) % above the critical one. At an angle of \(10^\circ\) the stress would be \(554\) MPa (NumPy). A steel column therefore does not carry substantially more than \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), although the elastic model would hold it further.

8.14.3 Column with pinned ends and other ways of support (steber z vrtljivima koncema in drugi načini podpiranja)

The column treated now has below a fixed pin support and above a movable one that slides along the axis and is pushed down by the force \(P\). The axis is again inextensible, but the departure from the straight line we describe here by a function \(v(x)\) along the straight line, because the boundary conditions are simpler. For the energy we must know by how much the upper support descends when the axis bends.

Lemma 8.133 Shortening of the axis and the work of the axial force (skrček osi in delo osne sile)

Let the axis of the column of length \(L\) be the graph of a function \(v\) on \([0, \ell]\), continuously differentiable with \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) and \(v(0) = v(\ell) = 0\), and let the length of the graph be \(L\), \(\int_0^\ell\sqrt{1 + v'^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = L\). Then the shortening \(\Delta = L - \ell\) lies between

\[\Big(1 - \frac{v'^2_{\max}}{4}\Big)\,\frac12\int_0^\ell v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ \le\ \Delta \ \le\ \frac12\int_0^\ell v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{8.121}\]

so the relative error of the approximation \(\Delta \approx \tfrac12\int v'^2\) is at most \(v'^2_{\max}/4 \le 0{,}25\) %. The compressive force \(P\), which points along the straight line between the supports and holds the top, has the potential energy \(-P\,\Delta \approx -\tfrac P2\int v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). A constant axial force \(N\) with the sign of definition 2.5 (tension positive) adds to the energy the term \(+\tfrac N2\int v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).

Proof

We must show an estimate of the difference between the arc length and the length on the straight line, and then the sign of the work.

  1. From \(\int_0^\ell\sqrt{1+v'^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = L\), \(\Delta = L - \ell = \int_0^\ell\big(\sqrt{1 + v'^2} - 1\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. For \(p \ge 0\), \(\sqrt{1 + p^2} - 1 = p^2/(\sqrt{1 + p^2} + 1)\). The denominator is at least \(2\), so \(\sqrt{1 + p^2} - 1 \le p^2/2\). From \((1 + p^2/2)^2 = 1 + p^2 + p^4/4 \ge 1 + p^2\), \(\sqrt{1 + p^2} \le 1 + p^2/2\), so the denominator is at most \(2 + p^2/2\) and \(\sqrt{1 + p^2} - 1 \ge \tfrac{p^2/2}{1 + p^2/4} \ge \tfrac{p^2}{2}\big(1 - \tfrac{p^2}{4}\big)\).
  3. Integration over \(x\) with \(p = |v'|\) gives (8.121) (lemma 3.39, point 4).
  4. The force \(P\) points downward, the top descends by \(\Delta\), so the work of the force is \(P\,\Delta\) and the potential energy of the force is \(-P\,\Delta\), as for a weight. For the axial force \(N\), \(P = -N\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. COOK §18.1 (PDF p. 654) obtains the same term differently: with fixed ends the element \(\mathrm{d}x\) lengthens by \(\tfrac12 v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and the axial force \(P\) (in this source tension positive) does work on this lengthening.

The limits of the integral in the lemma are \(0\) and \(\ell\), not \(L\). At a displacement of the middle \(a = 42\) mm and the shape \(v = a\sin(\pi x/L)\) with \(L = 2\) m, \(\Delta = a^2\pi^2/(4L) = 2{,}18\) mm, so \(\Delta/L = 0{,}11\) %. The integral over \([0, L]\) instead of over \([0, \ell]\) therefore differs from the integral in the lemma by a ratio of the order \(10^{-3}\), less than the limit \(0{,}25\) % in the lemma, and we exchange the limits.

For a column hinged at both ends, of length \(L\), the total potential energy is therefore

\[\Pi(v) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EI\,v''^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \frac P2\int_0^L v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad v(0) = v(L) = 0 . \tag{8.122}\]

The rotation at the ends is free, so the natural condition is \(M = EI\,v'' = 0\) (section 5.11.4). The functional is quadratic, so \(\Pi(\alpha\eta) = \alpha^2\Pi(\eta)\), the first variation at \(v = 0\) is zero (the straight position is an equilibrium for every \(P\)) and the second variation is \(\delta^2\Pi(0, \eta) = 2\,\Pi(\eta)\), that is

\[\delta^2\Pi(0, \eta) = \int_0^L \big(EI\,\eta''^2 - P\,\eta'^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{8.123}\]

The Euler-Lagrange equation (theorem 5.69 with \(F = \tfrac12 EI\,r^2 - \tfrac12 P\,p^2\)) is \(EI\,v'''' + P\,v'' = 0\), which is the equilibrium equation of a beam with axial force \(N = -P\) from the next section.

Theorem 8.134 Column with pinned ends (steber z vrtljivima koncema)

The second variation (8.123) is positive for every twice continuously differentiable function \(\eta \ne 0\) with \(\eta(0) = \eta(L) = 0\) exactly when

\[P < P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{L^2} . \tag{8.124}\]
Proof

We must show both directions, the first with corollary 8.128, the second with a sine.

  1. Let \(P < P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). By corollary 8.128, \(P\int\eta'^2 \le P\,(L/\pi)^2\int\eta''^2\), so \(\delta^2\Pi \ge \big(EI - P\,L^2/\pi^2\big)\int\eta''^2 = EI\,(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\int\eta''^2\).
  2. If \(\int\eta''^2 = 0\), then \(\eta'' = 0\), so by corollary 1.85 \(\eta'\) is constant and once more \(\eta\) is linear. By \(\eta(0) = \eta(L) = 0\), \(\eta = 0\). For \(\eta \ne 0\) therefore \(\int\eta''^2 > 0\) and \(\delta^2\Pi > 0\).
  3. Let \(P \ge P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). Take \(\eta = \sin(\pi x/L)\). By corollary 8.128, step 5, \(\int\eta''^2 = (\pi/L)^2\int\eta'^2\), so \(\delta^2\Pi = \big((\pi/L)^2 EI - P\big)\int\eta'^2 = (P_{\mathrm{cr}} - P)\int\eta'^2 \le 0\), because \(\int\eta'^2 > 0\).

Source: COOK §18.1 (PDF p. 654 to 655) obtains \(\pi^2 EI/L^2\) by the energy route, when he inserts the deflection in the form of a half sine (his sign is with tension positive, so he writes \(-\pi^2 EI/L^2\)), GR (4.266) (PDF p. 293) from the natural frequencies of a beam with axial force, when the first one vanishes, BOWER §10.4.3 (PDF p. 677) from the equilibrium equation. BOWER also states that the straight column is stable for \(P < \pi^2 EI_2/L^2\) with the smaller principal moment \(I_2\). The proof with the inequality is not from a source.

Since the functional is quadratic, \(\Pi(v) = \tfrac12\delta^2\Pi(0, v)\), so the straight position is energetically stable exactly for \(P < P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). A cantilever of length \(L\) has by equation (8.119) the same critical force as a column with pinned ends and length \(2L\). It must be so: if we mirror the cantilever across the clamp, we get a column with pinned ends and length \(2L\), and its first buckling shape \(\sin(\pi x/2L)\) has in the middle, that is at the clamp, a horizontal tangent. The strip with \(L = 2\) m has \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 12\,896\) N (NumPy) for buckling about the weak axis and \(51\,585\) N about the strong one. If both planes are possible, the displacements \(v\) (in direction \(y\), stiffness \(EI_{\mathrm{z}}\)) and \(w\) (in direction \(z\), stiffness \(EI_{\mathrm{y}}\)) are independent, since by lemma 8.133 the shortening with two displacements splits into the sum \(\tfrac12\int(v'^2 + w'^2)\). The second variation is the sum of both and becomes nonpositive first at the smaller threshold, so at the smaller of \(EI_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(EI_{\mathrm{z}}\). The column therefore twists about the principal axis with the smaller moment of inertia (corollary 5.31), for the strip about the axis \(y\).

Let us check the numbers from chapters 3 and 4. A bar of diameter 10 mm has \(I = \pi d^4/64 = 490{,}9\) mm⁴ and at \(L = 10\) m, \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/L^2 = 9{,}50\) N, which is the number from GR (4.266). The bar \(AC\) with area \(A = 1\) cm² of solid circular cross-section has \(I = A^2/(4\pi) = 795{,}8\) mm⁴, because from \(A = \pi d^2/4\) follows \(d^2 = 4A/\pi\) and \(I = \pi d^4/64 = A^2/(4\pi)\), and at \(L = 4\) m, \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 96{,}2\) N, which is \(139\) times less than the force \(13{,}33\) kN. A solid circular bar would for \(13{,}33\) kN need \(I = 110\,282\) mm⁴, so a diameter of \(38{,}7\) mm and an area of \(1177\) mm², twelve times more. Therefore for compressed bars we choose a cross-section with a larger moment of inertia at the same area, for example a tube. Both numbers from chapters 3 and 4 are thus confirmed.

What about other ways of support? The equilibrium equation is \(EI\,v'''' + P\,v'' = 0\) (EP (6.4.38), p. 361). With \(k^2 = P/EI\) it is solved by the family \(v = c_1 + c_2 x + c_3\sin kx + c_4\cos kx\), since \(EI\,v'''' = EI\,k^4(c_3\sin kx + c_4\cos kx) = -P\,v''\). The family reaches all initial values \((v, v', v'', v''')\) at \(x = 0\), because the matrix that connects them with the numbers \(c_1, \dots, c_4\) is invertible for \(k \ne 0\), and a linear equation of fourth order has by existence and uniqueness exactly one solution for given initial values (KREYSZIG §3.1, theorem 2, PDF p. 134, as in section 5.8.3). There is therefore no other solution. The four conditions at the ends give a system of four equations for the numbers \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\), which has a nonzero solution exactly when its determinant is zero (SymPy):

  • Clamped at both ends (\(v = v' = 0\)): the determinant is \(k\,\big(kL\sin kL + 2\cos kL - 2\big) = 4k\,\sin\tfrac{kL}{2}\,\big(\tfrac{kL}{2}\cos\tfrac{kL}{2} - \sin\tfrac{kL}{2}\big)\). The first zero is \(kL = 2\pi\), then at \(\tan(kL/2) = kL/2\) follows \(kL = 8{,}987\). The first threshold is \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 4\pi^2 EI/L^2\).
  • Clamped at \(x = 0\) and pin-supported at \(x = L\) (\(v = v' = 0\) at \(x = 0\), \(v = v'' = 0\) at \(x = L\)): the determinant is \(k^2\,(kL\cos kL - \sin kL)\), so \(\tan kL = kL\), the first positive zero is \(kL = 4{,}4934\). The threshold is \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 20{,}19\,EI/L^2\).

The zeros of the determinants tell at which forces the equilibrium equation with the boundary conditions has a curved solution. The smallest such force is the threshold \(P_1\), for both ends clamped \(4\pi^2 EI/L^2\), for the clamp and the pin \(20{,}19\,EI/L^2\). To show that the threshold is also the limit of stability we must show two things: above the threshold the second variation (8.123) (with the boundary conditions of the chosen support) is not positive for some \(\eta\), and below the threshold it is positive for every \(\eta \ne 0\). The first we show for both supports at once. Let \(v_1\) be the curved solution at \(P_1\). We multiply the equation \(EI\,v_1'''' + P_1 v_1'' = 0\) by \(v_1\) and integrate by parts (corollary 3.41): \(\int EI\,v_1''''\,v_1 = \big[EI\,v_1'''\,v_1 - EI\,v_1''\,v_1'\big]_0^L + \int EI\,v_1''^2\) and \(\int P_1 v_1''\,v_1 = \big[P_1 v_1'\,v_1\big]_0^L - P_1\int v_1'^2\). The terms at the ends vanish, because at each end \(v_1 = 0\) and \(v_1' = 0\) or \(v_1'' = 0\), so \(\int EI\,v_1''^2 = P_1\int v_1'^2\). At \(P \ge P_1\) therefore \(\int(EI\,v_1''^2 - P\,v_1'^2) = (P_1 - P)\int v_1'^2 \le 0\). At \(P > P_1\) the straight position is not stable. At \(P = P_1\) the second variation in the direction \(v_1\) is zero, and the energy (8.122) is quadratic, so the model does not decide on the limit itself. For that we would need the exact energy as for the cantilever in point (c) of theorem 8.131, which we do not do here.

The second, positivity below the threshold, we prove for both ends clamped with lemma 8.127, if we split the shape into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part with respect to the middle of the column. The symmetric part has a horizontal tangent in the middle, the antisymmetric part zero displacement in the middle, so we estimate each half with the inequality that we already have.

Theorem 8.135 Column with clamped ends (steber z vpetima koncema)

The second variation \(\int_0^L \big(EI\,\eta''^2 - P\,\eta'^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\) is positive for every twice continuously differentiable function \(\eta \ne 0\) with \(\eta(0) = \eta'(0) = \eta(L) = \eta'(L) = 0\) exactly when

\[P < P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \frac{4\pi^2 EI}{L^2} . \tag{8.125}\]
Proof

We must show that \(\int\eta'^2 \le (L/2\pi)^2\int\eta''^2\), and then both directions as for theorem 8.134. All integrals are over \([0, L]\).

  1. Let \(\tilde\eta(x) = \eta(L - x)\), \(a = (\eta + \tilde\eta)/2\) and \(b = (\eta - \tilde\eta)/2\). By the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 3), \(\tilde\eta'(x) = -\eta'(L - x)\) and \(\tilde\eta''(x) = \eta''(L - x)\), so \(a\) and \(b\) are twice continuously differentiable, \(\eta = a + b\), and both are zero with zero derivative at \(0\) and \(L\).
  2. We have \(a(L - x) = a(x)\) and \(b(L - x) = -b(x)\). Differentiation by the chain rule gives \(a'(L - x) = -a'(x)\), \(b'(L - x) = b'(x)\), \(a''(L - x) = a''(x)\) and \(b''(L - x) = -b''(x)\). At \(x = L/2\) it follows that \(a'(L/2) = 0\) and \(b(L/2) = 0\).
  3. Let \(f\) be continuous with \(f(L - x) = -f(x)\) and \(F\) its antiderivative. The function \(F(L - x)\) has the derivative \(-f(L - x) = f(x)\), so by the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40) \(\int_0^L f = F(L - L) - F(L - 0) = -\int_0^L f\), so \(\int_0^L f = 0\). The functions \(a'b'\) and \(a''b''\) have this property by step 2. Therefore \(\int\eta'^2 = \int a'^2 + \int b'^2\) and \(\int\eta''^2 = \int a''^2 + \int b''^2\).
  4. The function \(a'\) is continuously differentiable and zero at \(0\), \(L/2\) and \(L\) (steps 1 and 2). Lemma 8.127 in case (a) on \([0, L/2]\) and on \([L/2, L]\) (with the shift \(x = L/2 + t\)) with \(\ell = L/2\) and \(k = 2\pi/L\) gives \(\int a''^2 \ge (2\pi/L)^2\int a'^2\).
  5. The function \(b\) is twice continuously differentiable and zero at \(0\), \(L/2\) and \(L\). Corollary 8.128 on \([0, L/2]\) and on \([L/2, L]\) with the length \(L/2\) gives \(\int b'^2 \le (L/2\pi)^2\int b''^2\).
  6. By steps 3 to 5, \(\int\eta'^2 = \int a'^2 + \int b'^2 \le (L/2\pi)^2\big(\int a''^2 + \int b''^2\big) = (L/2\pi)^2\int\eta''^2\).
  7. Let \(P < P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). By step 6 the second variation is at least \(\big(EI - P\,(L/2\pi)^2\big)\int\eta''^2 = EI\,(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\int\eta''^2\). For \(\eta \ne 0\), \(\int\eta''^2 > 0\) as in step 2 of the proof of theorem 8.134, so the second variation is positive.
  8. Let \(P \ge P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) and \(\eta = 1 - \cos(2\pi x/L)\). It satisfies the four conditions, because \(\cos 0 = \cos 2\pi = 1\) and \(\sin 0 = \sin 2\pi = 0\), and \(\eta' = (2\pi/L)\sin(2\pi x/L)\), \(\eta'' = (2\pi/L)^2\cos(2\pi x/L)\). As in step 9 of the proof of lemma 8.127, here with \(\sin 4\pi = 0\), \(\int\sin^2(2\pi x/L) = \int\cos^2(2\pi x/L) = L/2\). The second variation is therefore \((2\pi/L)^2\,(L/2)\,\big(EI\,(2\pi/L)^2 - P\big) = (2\pi/L)^2\,(L/2)\,(P_{\mathrm{cr}} - P) \le 0\).

Source: The proof is not from a source.

The split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts showed why the threshold of clamped ends is four times that of pinned ends: each of the two halves resists like a column of half the length. For the clamp and the pin this split does not work, because the column is not symmetric. The conditions \(\eta(0) = \eta(L) = 0\) do hold, however, so by corollary 8.128, as in step 1 of the proof of theorem 8.134, we get a positive second variation for \(P < \pi^2 EI/L^2\), that is below \(0{,}489\) of the threshold \(20{,}19\,EI/L^2\). That it is positive all the way to the threshold is supported here only by a computation: the function \(kL\cos kL - \sin kL\) has no zero between \(0\) and \(kL = 4{,}4934\) (SymPy), so below the threshold there is no curved equilibrium. That positivity of the second variation follows from this is shown by the expansion in eigenfunctions in chapter 13.

For all four ways of support the critical force has the form \(\pi^2 EI/L_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) with the length \(L_{\mathrm{e}} = \pi\sqrt{EI/P_{\mathrm{cr}}} = \pi/k\), which we call the effective length (efektivna dolžina): \(L_{\mathrm{e}} = L\) for pinned ends, \(L/2\) for clamped ends, \(\pi L/4{,}4934 = 0{,}699\,L\) for the clamp and the pin and \(2L\) for the cantilever (figure 8.44). The name and the computation are ours, the sources of the project do not treat the effective length of a column. What does this length mean on the column? The moment in the buckling shape is \(M = EI\,v'' = -EI\,k^2\,(c_3\sin kx + c_4\cos kx)\), so it satisfies \(M'' + k^2 M = 0\). If \(M(x_0) = 0\), then by theorem 8.17 \(M(x) = \big(M'(x_0)/k\big)\sin k(x - x_0)\). The sine is zero exactly at multiples of the number \(\pi\) (lemma 8.10, point 3, and \(\sin(t + \pi) = -\sin t\) by the addition theorem), so adjacent zeros of the moment are \(\pi/k = L_{\mathrm{e}}\) apart. Between them the departure from the straight line \(c_1 + c_2 x\) equals \(c_3\sin kx + c_4\cos kx = -M/(EI\,k^2)\), so a half sine of length \(L_{\mathrm{e}}\), as for the column with pinned ends. The effective length is therefore the distance between adjacent points of zero moment: between the pinned ends, between the inflection points at \(x = L/4\) and \(3L/4\) for clamped ends, between the inflection at \(x = 0{,}301\,L\) and the pin for the clamp and the pin, and between the free top and its mirror image across the clamp for the cantilever. For the strip with \(L = 2\) m the critical forces for buckling about the weak axis are \(12{,}896\) kN, \(51{,}585\) kN and \(26{,}383\) kN, for the cantilever with \(L = 1\) m it is \(12{,}896\) kN.

As in Ritz's method (definition 6.32) the threshold can be estimated by choosing a trial function. For a column with pinned ends consider the quotient

\[R(\eta) = \frac{\int_0^L \eta''^2\,\mathrm{d}x}{\int_0^L \eta'^2\,\mathrm{d}x} , \tag{8.126}\]

which is called the Rayleigh quotient (Rayleighov količnik, chapter 10), as EP (p. 261) calls a similar quotient for the vibration of a bar. Corollary 8.128 says \(R(\eta) \ge \pi^2/L^2\) for every \(\eta\) with \(\eta(0) = \eta(L) = 0\), equality holds for the sine, so \(EI\,R(\eta)\) is for every trial function an upper bound of the critical force \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) (similar to BATHE example 3.24, PDF p. 140, where Ritz's method gives an approximation of the lowest critical force of a clamped column with a spring). The parabola \(x(L - x)\) gives \(R = 12/L^2\), which is \(21{,}6\) % above \(\pi^2/L^2\). The deflection of a uniformly loaded beam with pinned ends, \(v = x(L^3 - 2Lx^2 + x^3)\), gives \(R = 168/(17L^2)\), which is \(0{,}13\) % above. The sine is exact (SymPy). The deflection is such a good trial function because its shape is very close to the sine.

8.14.4 Axial force and bending (osna sila in upogib)

So far the compressive force was the only load. What happens if the column also has a transverse load \(q\) (positive upward) or if the axial force is tensile? Lemma 8.133 says that a constant axial force \(N\) adds to the energy the term \(\tfrac N2\int v'^2\), and this is exactly the term \(\tfrac12 c\,p^2\) with \(c = N\) from example 3 in section 5.11.3, which we announced there. The total energy of a beam with transverse load \(q\) is

\[\Pi(v) = \int_0^L \Big(\tfrac12\,EI\,v''^2 + \tfrac N2\,v'^2 - q\,v\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x ,\]

and its Euler-Lagrange equation (example 3 with \(k = 0\)) is

\[\begin{aligned} EI\,v'''' - N\,v'' &= q , \\ \text{at compression} (N = -P) : \quad EI\,v'''' + P\,v'' &= q . \end{aligned} \tag{8.127}\]

The sign matters: at tension (\(N > 0\)) the term \(-N\,v''\) has the opposite sign than at compression, so tension stiffens the beam.

Why does the deflection grow under compression? For a column with pinned ends take the load \(q = q_0\sin(\pi x/L)\). The deflection \(v = a\sin(\pi x/L)\) satisfies the boundary conditions (\(v = 0\) and \(M = EI\,v'' = 0\) at the ends) and the equation (8.127) if \(a\,\big(EI\,k^4 - P\,k^2\big) = q_0\) with \(k = \pi/L\). Since \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = EI\,k^2\),

\[a = \frac{q_0}{EI\,k^4\,(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})} = \frac{a_0}{1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}}} , \tag{8.128}\]

where \(a_0 = q_0/(EI\,k^4)\) is the deflection without axial force. This is exact for a sinusoidal load: the deflection grows toward infinity as the force approaches \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) (figure 8.45). At tension \(N = +0{,}5\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) the same computation gives \(a = a_0/(1 + N/P_{\mathrm{cr}}) = \tfrac23\,a_0\). A uniform load is not a sine, so the factor is not exact. The exact solution (SymPy) gives the deflection of the middle relative to the deflection without force \(1{,}3345\) at \(0{,}25\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) (against \(1/(1 - 0{,}25) = 1{,}3333\)), \(2{,}0036\) at \(0{,}5\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) (against \(2\)) and \(10{,}034\) at \(0{,}9\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) (against \(10\)). At \(0{,}9\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) the difference from the estimate is \(0{,}34\) %. The reason is that the uniform load is close in shape to a sine: the expansion in sines that chapter 13 brings has higher terms with critical forces \(m^2 P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) (\(m = 3, 5, \dots\)), which are amplified less. We get a useful estimate: the deflection under compression is approximately \(1/(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\) times the deflection without compression.

Real columns are not perfectly straight. If a column has an initial curvature or the force is eccentric, it bends already at a small force and the deflection grows quickly as the force approaches the limit (COOK Figure 18.1-2, PDF p. 655). For example B with an imperfection \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad (the spring is unstressed at this angle, example 8.66) the angle is \(0{,}0200\) rad at \(0{,}5\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), \(0{,}0986\) at \(0{,}9\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), \(0{,}342\) at \(0{,}99\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), \(0{,}392\) at \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) and \(0{,}621\) rad at \(1{,}05\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). The linear estimate \(\theta_0/(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\) is at \(0{,}9\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) higher by \(1{,}5\) % (\(0{,}1\) against \(0{,}0986\)), and at \(0{,}99\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) almost \(3\) times too large (\(1{,}0\) against \(0{,}342\)), because linearization assumes small angles. A real column always has some imperfection, so \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) is not a reliable estimate of its load capacity. COOK (PDF p. 655 and 656) warns that the critical force is correct only for a perfectly straight column, that linear analysis of bifurcation can strongly overestimate the capacity and that the failure force can be larger or smaller than the critical one. Rules for safety factors for columns the sources of the project do not contain, so we do not give them here.

The formula for the critical force holds only in the elastic range. The stress at the critical force is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} = P_{\mathrm{cr}}/A = \pi^2 E/\lambda^2\) with the slenderness (vitkost) \(\lambda = L/i\) and the radius of gyration \(i = \sqrt{I/A}\), which for the strip about the weak axis is \(5{,}774\) mm. At \(L = 2\) m, \(\lambda = 346\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} = 16{,}1\) MPa (figure 8.46). The stress reaches the yield limit \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa at \(\lambda_{\mathrm{Y}} = \pi\sqrt{E/\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}} = 93{,}8\), that is at the length \(L = 541\) mm (pin support). For shorter columns Euler's formula does not hold, because it violates assumption 1 of linear elasticity. Under pure compression steel starts to yield at the force \(A\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 176{,}0\) kN.

From history

Euler's formula for the column from section 5.9 was derived by Euler in 1744 for a column clamped at one end (TIMO, PDF p. 37, 41 to 42, 47). The constant \(C\) in it has the dimension of force times the square of length (TIMO, PDF p. 44), which is the dimension of the stiffness \(EI\) in our notation. In 1757 Euler published on columns again and gave a simple derivation of the formula for the critical load from a simplified differential equation (TIMO, PDF p. 44). In later writings he treated columns of variable cross-section and a column with an axial load distributed along the length, but did not arrive at the correct solutions (TIMO, PDF p. 44).

Lagrange found that an infinite set of buckling shapes is possible. For the shape with one half-wave a load four times larger than for Euler's column clamped at one end is needed, for the next sixteen times larger (TIMO, PDF p. 47). This agrees with our column with pinned ends, which has a critical force four times that of a cantilever of the same length, and with its second shape with sixteen times. He went further and investigated the deflection when the load exceeds the critical one. Instead of the approximate expression he used the exact expression for the curvature and integrated the equation by expansion in terms (TIMO, PDF p. 47). For small displacements the expansion converges quickly, so from it the load for a given displacement is easily computed (TIMO, PDF p. 47). This is the task that we solved above with the integral \(K(k)\) in theorem 8.132.

Musschenbroek made with compression experiments on bars the first practical investigation of sideways buckling and found that the critical load is inversely proportional to the square of the length of the bar (TIMO, PDF p. 63). This agrees with Euler's computation (TIMO, PDF p. 63), since the length in our \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/(4L^2)\) appears only in the denominator squared: the condition \(kL = \pi/2\) with \(k^2 = P/EI\) gives \(P \propto 1/L^2\).

Young treated a compressed prismatic column that is initially slightly curved in the shape of a half sine \(\delta_0\sin(\pi x/l)\), and obtained the deflection of the middle after the action of the compressive force \(P\), \(\delta = \delta_0/\big(1 - P l^2/(EI\pi^2)\big)\) (TIMO, PDF p. 103). From this he concluded that at \(P = EI\pi^2/l^2\) the deflection becomes infinite regardless of the size of \(\delta_0\), and this is the first derivation of the equation for a column that takes into account that it is not perfectly straight (TIMO, PDF p. 103). The same factor \(1/(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\) we obtained above for a sinusoidal transverse load. Young also pointed out that Euler's formula holds only for slender columns, and that shorter ones fail by crushing of the material and not by buckling (TIMO, PDF p. 103).

Reliable experiments were first made by Bauschinger: with conical attachments he ensured free rotation of the ends and central loading, and slender bars agreed with Euler's formula, while shorter ones buckled at compressive stresses above the elastic limit and Euler's theory is not applicable to them (TIMO, PDF p. 233). Tetmajer, after experiments on a large number of built-up iron and steel columns, recommended Euler's formula for structural steel at slenderness above 110 and a linear formula for shorter bars (TIMO, PDF p. 233). The limit is a property of the material, since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{Y}} = \pi\sqrt{E/\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}}\), so his number is not necessarily equal to our \(93{,}8\) for the steel of the book. Engesser proposed to extend Euler's formula by replacing the constant modulus \(E\) with a variable tangent modulus \(E_{\mathrm{t}} = \mathrm{d}\sigma/\mathrm{d}\varepsilon\), determined from the curve of the compression experiment, and so to compute critical stresses for bars outside the elastic range (TIMO, PDF p. 237). Jasinsky objected that during buckling the compressive stresses on the convex side decrease, so for this part of the cross-section the constant modulus \(E\) must be used and not \(E_{\mathrm{t}}\), in agreement with Bauschinger's experiments (TIMO, PDF p. 237). Engesser corrected the theory with two moduli for the two parts of the cross-section (TIMO, PDF p. 237).

Let us return to the column from the strip. Euler's formula holds for slenderness above \(93{,}8\), where the critical stress reaches the yield limit, and imperfections of shape enlarge the displacement already below the critical force. Below this slenderness we would need the tangent modulus instead of the modulus \(E\), which goes beyond the elastic model of this book.

The questions of the section now have answers. Buckling is the loss of positivity of the second variation of the energy: for the cantilever it is \(\int EI\,\eta'^2 - P\,\eta^2\), positive exactly below \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/(4L^2)\), for the column with pinned ends \(\int EI\,\eta''^2 - P\,\eta'^2\), positive exactly below \(\pi^2 EI/L^2\), and both follow from the inequality of lemma 8.127. For clamped ends, with the split into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part, the second variation is positive exactly below \(4\pi^2 EI/L^2\) (theorem 8.135), while for the clamp and the pin we proved positivity only below \(\pi^2 EI/L^2\), up to the threshold \(20{,}19\,EI/L^2\) it is supported by a computation. At the critical force itself the second variation does not decide: for the cantilever the straight position is still the lowest with the exact energy, for the other supports with the quadratic energy the question stays open. The strip at \(L = 2\) m with pin supports has the threshold \(12{,}896\) kN, 16 MPa, which the material withstands without difficulty, and the threshold does not come from the strength of the material. The numbers \(9{,}5\) N and \(0{,}1\) kN from chapters 3 and 4 are computed from \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/L^2\).

8.15 Connections (povezave)

The abbreviations of the courses are the same as in section 1.19.

  • Lagrange's equations and small oscillations: one degree of freedom with damping and excitation (VD 5-6, DSK, chapter 9), also impulse loading (GR §1.5), \(n\) degrees of freedom and modes of oscillation (VD 7-10, chapter 10), damping models (chapter 20), modal reduction (chapter 21).
  • Hamilton's principle for a continuum: strings, shafts and beams (VD 11-12, DSK 2, chapter 13), plates (chapter 18).
  • A rigid body in space and gyroscopic forces (chapter 24), crank mechanisms (chapter 23), manipulators with Lagrange's equations (DSK 13, chapter 27, SPONG).
  • Constraints and multipliers in the finite element method, the penalty method and multipliers (chapters 12 and 19), geometric stiffness and linear buckling analysis (chapter 12, COOK, chapter 18).
  • Stability of plates: buckling of a circular plate (EP §7.2.2.2, p. 411 to 414) and of a rectangular plate (EP §7.2.4.3, p. 445 to 447, and §7.2.8, p. 476 to 485), chapter 18. Stability of shells the sources of the project do not treat.
